One case is recorded: on 8 January 2019 the National Court of Justice sentenced former bank president Pedro Delgado to five years in prison, restitution of $788,855.94 and forfeiture of assets. The prosecutor's office called the crime unlawful association; the court's own post called it illicit enrichment. The source reports government pressure in 2 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018. Ecuador has had 2 systemic banking crises since 1970.
p:CMR: Cameroon's money, the Central African CFA franc, is issued by the Bank of Central African States (BEAC), which sets monetary policy for 6 members. The franc is fixed at EUR 1 = 655.957 CFA francs, France guarantees its convertibility, and the BEAC must keep at least 50% of its foreign reserves at the French Treasury. The bank scores 42 of 100 for outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed. One case is recorded: a November 2009 internal report found about 20 billion CFA francs diverted from the bank's Paris office to 139 beneficiaries between 2004 and 2008. On 28 September 2012 a court in Mfoundi sentenced Kemadjou to life imprisonment and ordered him to pay BEAC 26.4 billion CFA francs. Jean-Pierre Oyiba is named as a recipient of the money.
p:HKG: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority runs the Hong Kong dollar under a currency board, meaning the money is tied to another currency. Since 1983 it has been linked to the US dollar; since May 2005 the bank sells HK dollars at 7.75 and buys at 7.85 per US dollar. The bank scores 32 of 100 for outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed. One case is recorded: in 2012 a Legislative Council subcommittee said former chief Joseph Yam Chi-kwong should bear "ultimate responsibility" for investors' losses on Lehman minibonds. The HKMA replied that the report had not fully taken into account the information it submitted. It has 3 swap lines (agreements to borrow another central bank's currency), including a standing CNY 800 billion line with China.
p:SSD: The Bank of South Sudan is the central bank that issues the South Sudanese pound. It scores 37 of 100 for outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed; its weakest side is corruption in the country. Two cases are recorded. In February-March 2026 security forces detained former governor Manguak, under house arrest, with former finance ministers; no charges had been announced as of March 2026, and Manguak denies the allegations. A UN commission report said De La Rue transferred about $1.4 million in 2016-2017 to an Equity Bank account in Nairobi held by a bank consultant, against a banknote contract worth about $144 million, and noted suspected corruption. The UK Serious Fraud Office closed its investigation in June 2020 without charges. De La Rue prints the bank's banknotes.
p:ROU: The National Bank of Romania is the central bank that issues the Romanian leu. It scores 23 of 100 for outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed, making it less exposed than 90% of 194 places scored. One case is recorded. In 2014 the High Court of Cassation and Justice placed deputy governor Olteanu under 30-day house arrest in a National Anticorruption Directorate case alleging he received a EUR 1 million bribe in 2008 from businessman Sorin Ovidiu Vântu while parliament speaker. This is an allegation; the record lists the conviction as annulled as time-barred. The bank is part-owner of the Bank for International Settlements, which 63 central banks own. Its one swap line (an agreement to borrow another central bank's currency), with the European Central Bank, ended on 15 January 2024.
p:MMR: The Central Bank of Myanmar issues the kyat (MMK). Myanmar scores 55 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed; that is 3rd of 194 places. Its weakest side is corruption and secrecy, with a corruption index score of 16 of 100 and the top money-laundering risk rank (1 of 177). Government pressure was reported in 18 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, mostly to cut rates or ease and to print money. In December 2022 a junta court sentenced former deputy governor Bo Bo Nge to 20 years in prison; the junta-backed Anti-Corruption Commission accused him of not collecting tax on a $5 million deposit and placing a $350 million loan in a lower-interest account. The junta also replaced the governor and a vice chairman. Giesecke+Devrient suspended banknote supplies to the state printer after the military crackdown.
p:KNA: St. Kitts and Nevis does not issue its own money. The Eastern Caribbean Central Bank (ECCB) issues the EC dollar for 8 members and sets monetary policy for them. The EC dollar has been fixed at EC$2.70 to US$1.00 since July 1976, and the law requires reserves of at least 60% of currency in circulation. The country scores 29 of 100 on exposure to influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed. No government pressure on the bank was reported from 2010 to 2018. One case is on record. After the ECCB seized the Stanford-owned Bank of Antigua, the Official Stanford Investors Committee sued the ECCB in Dallas in 2013, alleging it misappropriated assets belonging to Stanford's victims and creditors. On 17 August 2018 a US federal judge dismissed the claims in full, because the ECCB and Antigua are immune under US foreign sovereign immunity law.
p:GTM: The Bank of Guatemala issues the quetzal (GTQ) and holds it close to a fixed rate against the US dollar. The country scores 32 of 100 on exposure to influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed; its weakest side is secrecy about who owns money and corruption (index score 26 of 100). No government pressure was reported from 2010 to 2018. In May 2015 Banguat president Julio Suárez was arrested with other board members of the social security institute (IGSS). Prosecutors said they took part in the irregular award of a 116 million quetzal (about $14.5 million) IGSS contract to the drug company Pisa de Guatemala. The Public Ministry and CICIG investigated. Suárez was later acquitted: the Supreme Court's Criminal Chamber upheld the June 2019 appeal-court acquittal, as reported in October 2021. The bank holds 15.5 tonnes of gold.
p:CIV: Côte d'Ivoire uses the West African CFA franc (XOF), issued by the Central Bank of West African States (BCEAO) for 8 members. The franc is fixed at 655.957 to the euro, and France guarantees to advance euros to the bank if its reserves run out. A 2019 agreement ended the rule that the BCEAO keep at least 50% of its reserves at the French Treasury. Exposure to influence scores 39 of 100, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed. Two cases date from 2010-2011. On 18 January 2018 a court convicted Laurent Gbagbo and three others of group theft of BCEAO vaults and cash, with 20-year sentences and a 329 billion CFA franc fine. Governor Dacoury-Tabley resigned in January 2011 after being criticized for ignoring a finance ministers' decision that gave Alassane Ouattara power over the bank.
p:SEN: Senegal uses the West African CFA franc (XOF), issued by the Central Bank of West African States (BCEAO) for 8 members. The franc is fixed at 655.957 to the euro, and France guarantees to advance euros to the bank if its reserves run out. A 2019 agreement ended the rule that the BCEAO keep at least 50% of its reserves at the French Treasury. Senegal scores 36 of 100 on exposure to influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed. No government pressure was reported from 2010 to 2018. One case is recorded: in January 2011 a summit of UEMOA heads of state accepted governor Dacoury-Tabley's resignation. He was criticized for ignoring a 23 December decision by finance ministers that gave Alassane Ouattara power over the bank, and the article says the BCEAO paid 60 to 100 billion CFA francs to the Gbagbo regime after that date.
p:CAN: The Bank of Canada issues the Canadian dollar, which moves within a band of 2% or less against the US dollar. Canada scores 20 of 100 on exposure to influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed; that is 187th of 194, among the least exposed. No documented case at the bank was found, and no government pressure was reported from 2010 to 2018. It is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. EY and PwC audit its accounts, and Canadian Bank Note Company and BA International print its notes. The Canadian dollar is 5.76% of world currency trading and 2.47% of foreign reserves, and the bank has 9 swap lines, which are agreements to borrow another central bank's currency.
p:AGO: The National Bank of Angola issues the kwanza (AOA). Angola scores 41 of 100 on exposure to influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed; its weakest side is secrecy about who owns money and corruption (index score 32 of 100). Government pressure was reported in 29 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, nearly all pressing the bank to cut rates or ease, with 8 threats to replace leaders. On 14 August 2020 the Supreme Court convicted former governor Valter Filipe (eight years), BNA manager Samalia (five years), José Filomeno dos Santos (five years) and businessman Sebastião (six years) of embezzlement, fraud and influence peddling over an attempted transfer of $500 million to a London account, which a British bank blocked. The Constitutional Court is also named in the case.
p:PER: The Central Reserve Bank of Peru issues the sol (PEN), managed within a band of about 5% against the US dollar. Peru scores 25 of 100 on exposure to influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed. No government pressure was reported from 2010 to 2018. The bank is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. One case, from 1986 to 1991, is alleged and unproven. A 1991 New York grand-jury indictment of BCCI, a bank, alleged $3 million in bribes in return for depositing part of Peru's 1986-87 reserves in BCCI's Panama branch; the Peruvian bank's board approved moving $100 million and later doubling it. The indictment did not name bank officials. The Christian Science Monitor identified Figueroa and Neyra, and both strenuously denied the charges.
p:SLE: The Bank of Sierra Leone issues the leone (SLE). Sierra Leone scores 36 of 100 on exposure to influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed. Under the 2019 Bank of Sierra Leone Act, sacking the governor needs a two-thirds majority in parliament. In August 2018 the newly elected president dismissed the governor, and Kelfala Kallon became the bank's third governor in 17 months. On 13 March 2023 President Julius Maada Bio sent Kallon on 'indefinite leave' and named deputy Ibrahim Stevens interim head; the article reports no official reason and says the president tried to bypass the 2019 Act. Separately, Kallon told Parliament on 22 November 2021 that he 'bribed' people hoarding the leone. The Anti-Corruption Commission investigated and said in May 2022 he meant cash swap operations selling about US$68.6 million in foreign currency, and that the word was used in error, and it closed the investigation.
p:TZA: The Bank of Tanzania issues the Tanzanian shilling. It scores 31 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and government pressure on it was reported in 2 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018. An audit by Ernst & Young of the bank's External Payment Arrears account found about 133 billion shillings paid out wrongly in 2005 and 2006 to 22 local companies, many phoney or using fake documents. President Jakaya Kikwete dismissed governor Ballali in January 2008, the companies were ordered to refund the money, and some lower-level defendants were jailed. In the first court cases to follow, reported on 27 May 2011, the Kisutu Resident Magistrate's Court in Dar es Salaam jailed the businessmen Farijala Hussein and Rajabu Maranda for five years and ordered them to return what they had taken. In 2024 the printing firms De La Rue and Crane Currency won the bank's tender to reprint its banknotes.
p:YEM: The Central Bank of Yemen issues the rial, held close to a fixed rate against the US dollar. It scores 43 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and the corruption and secrecy around it stand at 86. Government pressure was reported in 6 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, all of it pressing for easier money or for printing money. On 18 September 2016 President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi, announcing from Saudi Arabia, sacked central bank head Mohammed bin Hammam, named Mansar al-Kaiti in his place and ordered the bank moved to Aden, with no official reason given. On 6 December 2021 he dismissed the governor and his deputy, the fourth such sacking since the civil war began. A UN Panel of Experts report in January 2021 said the Aden-based bank broke its foreign-exchange rules and laundered 'a substantial part' of a 2 billion dollar Saudi deposit, giving traders a 423 million dollar windfall. The bank rejected the claims, and on 25 March 2021, after an internal review, the panel withdrew the money-laundering and corruption accusations.
p:TUN: The Central Bank of Tunisia issues the dinar (TND), which follows a pre-announced crawling peg, a slowly adjusted fixed rate, against the euro. Tunisia scores 28 of 100 on exposure to influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed. On 27 June 2012 President Moncef Marzouki fired governor Mustapha Kamel Nabli, alleging he had refused to bring monetary policy in line with the country's economic needs; the elected assembly approved the move in July 2012. In February 2018 Tunisian prosecutors said five bank agents were arrested, two of them jailed, in a currency-trafficking investigation. They were accused of money laundering, corruption and abuse of power for exchanging small euro notes for 200 and 500 euro notes without recording the operations. The central bank said it had referred the operations to the courts. The accusations are unproven.
p:LSO: Lesotho issues the loti (LSL), and the South African rand (ZAR) also circulates. Under the Common Monetary Area agreement, member currencies are pegged to the rand at par, meaning one for one, and Lesotho must fully back its currency issues with rand assets. The country scores 30 of 100 on exposure to influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed. One case is on record. In February 2024 three South Africans appeared in the Ficksburg Magistrates Court on fraud and money laundering charges over R57 million allegedly stolen from the Central Bank of Lesotho. The Hawks, a South African police unit, said Lesotho officials intercepted vouchers meant for service providers and diverted the payments to co-conspirators in South Africa. The charges are unproven. South Africa's Financial Intelligence Centre is also named in the case.
p:KGZ: The National Bank of the Kyrgyz Republic issues the som and keeps it within 2 percent of the US dollar. It scores 29 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. In September 2005 prosecutors placed governor Sarbanov under house arrest, accusing him of abuse of power for handing more than $400,000 to the deposed president Askar Akayev in 1999. Sarbanov denied wrongdoing, and on 26 April 2006 Judge Esenjan Abylkasymov acquitted him and four other former finance officials, ruling that there was no crime because they had acted in the interests of the state; the prosecutor's office said it would appeal. Two heads have left since. Parliament approved the early resignation of Kubanychbek Bokontaev on 26 June 2024, and Melis Turgunbaev, in the post from that same day, submitted his own resignation on 18 March 2026. No reason was given in either case.
p:NAM: The Bank of Namibia is the central bank of Namibia, which is in the Common Monetary Area with South Africa, Lesotho and Eswatini. Its currency is pegged to the rand at par, and Namibia must fully back its currency issues with rand assets. Namibia joined the current agreement in February 1992. The bank scores 26 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. One case from 2002 is alleged and unresolved. Court papers in a suit brought by Nambib Resources against the Minister of Mines listed governor Tom Alweendo as a 10 per cent shareholder in Trade Line Namibia, which had been given an exclusive prospecting licence on the Skeleton Coast. Alweendo said he was made a director of the company without his knowledge. The article reports no finding or outcome.
p:KHM: The National Bank of Cambodia is the country's central bank. Cambodia scores 36 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. Neither of the two matters on record was ever confirmed. The Phnom Penh Post reported that governor Thor Peng Leath made a three million US dollar central bank loan on 31 May 1994 so Credit Bank of Cambodia could meet its minimum capital, which bank officials called highly irregular, and that on 8 May 1995 the bank let 145,000 dollars out of former commerce minister Var Huot's frozen account. Var Huot denied preferential treatment, and no charges or findings followed. In November 2013 Chea Serey, daughter of governor Chea Chanto, was promoted to director-general; Tioulong Saumura, a former deputy governor, said being the governor's daughter should exclude her, citing nepotism, while Nguon Sokha called her a skilled technocrat. No investigation followed.
p:BLR: The National Bank of the Republic of Belarus issues the Belarusian ruble and holds it within 2 percent of a mix of the euro, the Russian ruble and the US dollar. It scores 31 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. In December 2016 the state security service, the KGB, said a directorate head at the bank and his deputy had been arrested over a bribe, reported as 13,000 dollars, for choosing the company BelAVM as an equipment supplier; the matter is unproven. At a trial reported in March 2020 prosecutors charged Feliks Kasperovich and Andrei Podgorny of the bank's information technology directorate with taking at least $868,750 in bribes from 2007 onwards, and Igor Kudasov, head of its payment systems directorate, with taking $30,000. Kasperovich admitted the charges in full; the rest remains unproven. Belarus also has two agreements with China, from 2010 and 2015, to borrow its currency.
p:GMB: The Central Bank of The Gambia scores 30 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. The Janneh Commission, a government inquiry into the finances of former president Yahya Jammeh, found that governor Amadou Colley let Jammeh and General Sulayman Badjie withdraw funds without proper authorisation, including millions of dollars by Badjie. The government's White Paper on the inquiry accepted that between September 2015 and January 2017 Badjie instructed the governor or his deputies to release US dollars, and that cash was handed over by the governor to soldiers and loaded into vehicles. It held Badjie accountable for $15,785,601, 300,000 euros and D9,606,000, ordered it recovered by selling his properties, and recorded a further $28.5 million wrongly granted in one bank account in 2000 and 2001 and $268,000 taken from the bank to buy the Observer newspaper. Colley was banned from public office for life and held jointly liable. Before the commission on 19 September 2017 he said accounts controlled by the Office of the President were opened at the bank, that one for sand mining was opened at that office's request, and that withdrawals followed instructions from someone there without the account signatory's approval.
p:MUS: The Bank of Mauritius issues the Mauritian rupee (MUR), which it keeps within 2% or less of the US dollar. Its exposure score is 25 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed. Written independence scores 0.733 of 1 on Romelli's 42 rules, and the bank has a swap line, an agreement to borrow another central bank's currency, with China for CNY 2 billion (MUR 13 billion), signed 4 September 2024. One case is recorded. On 9-10 April 2025 the Financial Crimes Commission arrested former governor Seegolam for 'fraud by abuse of position'; he was charged with fraud and released on bail. The investigation concerns the alleged embezzlement of 300 million rupees ($6.7 million) from the Mauritius Investment Corporation, a central bank-owned vehicle set up during the COVID pandemic. The charge is unproven.
p:ISL: The Central Bank of Iceland issues the króna (ISK), which it keeps within 2% or less of the euro. Its exposure score is 16 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed. It ranks 9th of 112 on transparency. It is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, and has a swap line with China, an agreement to borrow another central bank's currency, for CNY 3.5 billion (ISK 70 billion), dated 16 October 2025 for five years. In April 2010 the parliament's Special Investigation Commission found that seven officials, including central bank head Oddsson and central bank officials Gudnason and Fridriksson, acted with gross negligence before the 2008 collapse of Iceland's three largest banks, failing to act on information about the banks' condition.
p:DNK: Danmarks Nationalbank issues the Danish krone (DKK), which it holds in a pre-announced peg to the euro, a fixed rate announced in advance. Its exposure score is 16 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed. Its law was last changed in 1942. Its total assets were $109.8 billion at the end of 2025, 22.4% of GDP. It is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. PwC signed the auditor's report on its 2025 accounts, and Oberthur Fiduciaire was selected as banknote supplier under a four-year framework, with first notes in circulation in 2020. It has swap lines, agreements to borrow another central bank's currency, with the United States (up to USD 30 billion, 2020, expired 31 December 2021) and the European Central Bank (EUR 24,000 million). No documented case at the bank was found.
p:BWA: The Bank of Botswana issues the pula (BWP), which it manages against the South African rand through a pre-announced crawling peg or a narrow moving band. Its exposure score is 23 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed. Written independence scores 0.579 of 1 on Romelli's 42 rules. One case is recorded. A woman arrested on 17 October 2019 was implicated, with others including former president Ian Khama and former intelligence head Isaac Kgosi, in allegedly stealing P100 billion from the bank. The Directorate on Corruption and Economic Crime and the Directorate of Public Prosecutions are named in the case. High Court Judge Zein Kebonang discharged and acquitted her of unexplained property and a false passport declaration, and the state withdrew a terrorism financing charge. The allegations against the others are unproven.
p:KWT: The Central Bank of Kuwait issues the Kuwaiti dinar (KWD), which it holds in a pre-announced peg to the US dollar. Its exposure score is 32 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed. It scores 3 of 15 on transparency (99th of 112). Its total assets were $36.4 billion at the end of 2025, and it is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. One case is recorded, unconfirmed: the newspaper Al Jarida, citing unnamed sources, reported that the Capital Markets Authority had decided to refer Governor Mohammad Al Hashel to prosecutors for suspected breach of investment rules over shares in a local bank. He denied it, saying he had never traded shares in a listed company during his senior posts.
p:EGY: The Central Bank of Egypt issues the Egyptian pound (EGP), which it keeps within 2% or less of the US dollar. Its exposure score is 30 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed. Written independence scores 0.64 of 1 on Romelli's 42 rules. Government pressure was reported in 1 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, a threat to replace leaders. On 17 August 2022 governor Tarek Amer, whose term was due to run to 2023, resigned; President al-Sisi accepted the resignation and named him a presidential adviser, with the pound at 19.1 to the dollar. Daily News Egypt separately reported, without confirmation, severe pressure from no named source in October 2015. It has swap lines (agreements to borrow another central bank's currency) with China and the United Arab Emirates. No documented case of wrongdoing was found.
p:SOM: Somalia's money is the Somali shilling, and its central bank is the Central Bank of Somalia, the institution that issues the currency and holds the government's funds. Two cases are recorded. In 2013 governor Abrar resigned after seven weeks. She wrote to the president that from her appointment she had been asked to sanction deals and violate her fiduciary responsibility, and said she had refused to approve a contract over frozen government assets with the US law firm Shulman Rogers, which denied wrongdoing. Separately, a July 2013 report by the United Nations Monitoring Group for Somalia and Eritrea said 80% of withdrawals from the bank were made for private purposes and that the governor was key to the irregularities. It also said $12 million of $16.9 million transferred by the accounting firm PricewaterhouseCoopers could not be traced. The central bank rejected the allegations, and the report is listed as an official finding. The bank scores 37 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. Its weakest side is corruption in the country.
p:GNQ: Equatorial Guinea uses the Central African CFA franc (XAF), issued by the Bank of Central African States (BEAC), which sets monetary policy for 6 members. The franc is fixed at EUR 1 = 655.957 CFA francs. France guarantees convertibility without limit, and the BEAC must deposit at least 50% of its foreign exchange reserves at the French Treasury (lowered from 65% in 2007). Exposure score is 46 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed. The BEAC scores 0.5 of 15 on transparency, last of 112, and government pressure to cut rates or ease was reported in 3 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case: a November 2009 internal report found about 20 billion CFA francs diverted from the Paris office to 139 beneficiaries between 2004 and 2008. On 28 September 2012 a court in Mfoundi, Cameroon, sentenced Kemadjou to life imprisonment and ordered him to pay BEAC 26.4 billion CFA francs.
p:NIC: Nicaragua's money is issued by the Central Bank of Nicaragua. It scores 29 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. One case is recorded, covering 2000 to 2008, with an official finding. In 2007 the country's Comptroller General, the state auditor, concluded that the bank's board sold CENI certificates, which were issued to cover the collapse of banks, for less than market value. It then raised interest rates to benefit the main buyer, Bancentro. The fraud is described as 500 million dollars. The Comptroller alleged criminal involvement by six men, including former finance minister Eduardo Montealegre, who denied wrongdoing and called it a political witch hunt. In July 2008 a special prosecutor filed charges against 39 people including Montealegre. The report names no central bank officials among the accused and gives no court ruling. It says former bank president Francisco Mayorga had already been found guilty in the banking scandal.

p:BIH: Bosnia and Herzegovina's money, the convertible mark (BAM), is issued by the Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina under a currency board: marks are issued only against convertible foreign currency, at EUR 1 = KM 1.95583. The bank is a part-owner of the Bank for International Settlements, which only central banks own. Its law scores 0.899 of 1 on independence (Romelli), ranking 11 of 155, and no government pressure was reported in 2010-2018. On the map's scale, 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; it scores 35. One case is documented, from 2023: a criminal complaint accused governor Senad Softić of suspected wrongdoing in several cases, including a project to acquire an office building in Pale and a procedure to buy land in Sarajevo. The BiH Prosecutor's Office said in February 2023 that it had opened a case and was verifying the allegations. Nothing is proven.
p:MDA: The National Bank of Moldova issues the leu, which is held within 2% of the euro. Its law scores 0.861 of 1 for independence from government, and it scores 28 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Dorin Dragutanu resigned as governor on 21 September 2015 after criticism for failing to prevent about 1 billion dollars disappearing from three Moldovan banks in 2014; he said he was going because of political pressure, denied responsibility and said he had repeatedly warned the authorities. On 5 March 2020 prosecutors searched the bank's headquarters and detained deputy governor Cincilei, former deputy governor Tabirta and a division head on suspicion of fraud and money laundering tied to that theft, which surfaced after the bank made a 13 billion leu emergency loan later converted into public debt; they also moved to arrest Dragutanu. None of it is proven. On the evening of 21 December parliament dismissed governor Octavian Armasu, in post since November 2018, with 81 members in favour, citing 'insufficient and defective work' by the bank in examining the fraud case.
p:ZMB: The Bank of Zambia issues the kwacha (ZMW), which floats within a de facto band of about 5% against the US dollar. Its law scores 0.637 of 1 on independence (Romelli), ranking 104 of 155. On the map's scale, 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; Zambia scores 32. On 22 August 2020 President Edgar Lungu dismissed governor Denny Kalyalya, less than a week after he warned of economic difficulties, and appointed Christopher Mvunga from the finance ministry. In October 2015 the Drug Enforcement Commission arrested a bank section officer for theft by a public servant and money laundering, accused of taking USD 43,660 and K20,335 in cash between January and September 2015. The report gives no court outcome, so the accusation is unproven.
p:MAR: Bank Al-Maghrib issues Morocco's dirham (MAD), which is held to a pre-announced peg against the euro, meaning a fixed rate. Its law scores 0.768 of 1 on independence (Romelli), ranking 59 of 155, and no government pressure was reported in 2010-2018. On the map's scale, 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; Morocco scores 26. Two cases are documented, both under investigation and unproven. In 2022 the bank filed a complaint with the prosecutor's office against one of its staff and a service provider over suspected corruption in awarding contracts. On 4 July 2019 it said 1.2 million dirhams ($125,000) was stolen while cash moved from the Dar As-Sikkah mint to cities in the north; no findings or arrests were reported. It has a swap line (an agreement to borrow another central bank's currency) with China for 10 billion yuan ($1.53 billion), 2016-05; whether it is in force is not known.
p:LAO: The Bank of the Lao P.D.R. is the central bank of Laos, which uses the kip. One case is recorded and it ended in convictions. On 8 September 2026 the Vientiane People's Court sentenced two former directors general of the bank to life imprisonment. The court found they abused their positions to withdraw foreign currency from the bank's reserves and exchange unlimited amounts. One of them, Aod, was sentenced in his absence because he died during the proceedings. In a related case nine bank employees were convicted of corruption and money laundering, including trading currency at special rates. Losses across the cases exceeded 2.29 trillion kip ($102.6 million). Government pressure on the bank was reported in 1 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, and that pressure was a demand to print money. The bank has two swap lines with China, which are agreements to lend each other currency. One is for 6 billion yuan; the other has no amount stated. The bank scores 37 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed.
p:TON: The National Reserve Bank of Tonga issues the pa'anga (TOP), which follows a crawling peg or a band of 1% or less against the US dollar. It scores 5.5 of 15 on what it tells the public. On the map's scale, 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; Tonga scores 31. Two cases are documented. In 2024-2025 Tonga's Anti-Corruption Commissioner sued the bank and its directors, alleging that a 2024 staff payment (for example $6,600 to each of 73 staff) was an unlawful bonus linked to record profit; the board had described it as a one-off anniversary payout, and on 20 November 2025 the Court of Appeal dismissed the proceeding. In 2017-2019 a Senior Exchange Control Officer forged a Government bond to support another person's New Zealand visa application and asked for $2,500 pa'anga. She pleaded guilty and her employment was terminated; the Supreme Court of Tonga ruled on 21 May 2019.
p:ALB: The Bank of Albania is the central bank of Albania, which uses the lek. One case is recorded. In July 2014 a central bank employee was found to have stolen 713 million lek (nearly $7 million) from the bank's reserves. On 5 September 2014 prosecutors arrested governor Fullani and the bank's senior auditor and charged them with abuse of office for alleged mismanagement linked to the theft. The board dismissed Fullani. The charges are allegations, and no verdict is reported. The lek is a de facto peg to the euro, meaning it is held close to the euro without a formal commitment. The bank has a swap line with China for 2 billion yuan, signed on 3 April 2018, and had a temporary repo line with the European Central Bank from 15 December 2022 to 15 January 2024, which has expired. Government pressure on the bank was reported in none of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018. It scores 23 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed.
p:KAZ: The National Bank of Kazakhstan issues the tenge (KZT), which floats within a de facto band of about 5% against the US dollar. Gold is 77% of its reserves, 368.4 tonnes. Its law scores 0.716 of 1 on independence (Romelli), ranking 78 of 155. On the map's scale, 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; Kazakhstan scores 27. On 2 November 2015 President Nursultan Nazarbayev replaced chairman Kayrat Kelimbetov with presidential adviser Daniyar Akishev, telling parliament that confidence in the bank and the tenge had fallen and that tenge liquidity was short. The article carries no statement from Kelimbetov. It has 5 swap lines (agreements to borrow another central bank's currency), including Türkiye (TRY 28.0 billion, 2025), Russia (RUB 35 billion, 28 May 2026) and China (7 billion yuan, 14 December 2014).
p:TGO: Togo uses the CFA franc (XOF), issued by the Central Bank of West African States (BCEAO), which sets monetary policy for 8 member countries. The currency is fixed at EUR 1 = 655.957 CFA francs, and France guarantees it by lending to the BCEAO if its foreign exchange reserves run out. A cooperation agreement signed on 21 December 2019 replaced the 1973 one and ended the rule that the BCEAO keep at least 50% of its reserves at the French Treasury. On a scale where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, the bank scores 40, its weakest side being corruption and money-laundering risk around it. One case is recorded: governor Dacoury-Tabley resigned in January 2011 after being criticized for ignoring a 23 December 2010 decision of finance ministers; the source says the BCEAO paid 60 to 100 billion CFA francs to the Gbagbo regime afterward.
p:CZE: The Czech National Bank issues the koruna (CZK) and scores 18 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed. That makes it less exposed than 97% of the 194 places scored. Its written independence scores are 0.795 of 1 (Romelli) and 0.832 of 1 (Garriga). It belongs to the Bank for International Settlements, which is owned only by central banks, and Ernst & Young Audit, s.r.o. audits its accounts. The one recorded case dates from 2026: police arrested a long-time employee accused of misappropriating tens of millions of koruna, after suspicious transactions at its Brno branch were flagged. It is under investigation and nothing is proven. Government pressure was reported in 3 of 37 quarters in 2010 to 2018, all threats to replace leaders and calls to tighten.
p:ETH: The National Bank of Ethiopia issues the birr (ETB). It scores 32 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, which is more exposed than 61% of the 194 places scored. Its legal independence is low: 0.495 of 1 on Romelli's 42 rules and 0.291 of 1 on the Garriga measure, rank 176 of 191. Government pressure was reported in 3 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, mostly pressing to cut rates or ease. One case is recorded. In March 2008 Ethiopian anti-corruption officials arrested 26 people after 90 kilos of fake gold were found in the bank's vaults: 7 from the bank, 4 from the Ethiopian Geological Survey and 15 businessmen and collaborators. The report covers arrests only, not charges or court outcomes.
p:GBR: The Bank of England is the central bank of the United Kingdom and issues the pound sterling. Two cases are recorded. Deputy governor Charlotte Hogg resigned on 14 March 2017 after the House of Commons Treasury Committee reported that her failure, on several occasions since she joined the Bank in 2013, to declare that her brother was director of group strategy at the bank Barclays was a very serious breach; she said she had also unintentionally misled the committee. The Bank also referred material on its 2007 and 2008 liquidity auctions to the Serious Fraud Office, which investigated from 2015 and closed the matter in June 2017, finding no evidence of criminality. Officials move both ways between the Bank and private finance, with 18 such moves on file. Mervyn King joined Citigroup as a senior adviser after retiring as governor in 2013, and Mark Carney became vice chair of Brookfield Asset Management in August 2020. Ben Broadbent and Huw Pill were chief or senior European economists at Goldman Sachs before joining, and Katharine Braddick moves from Barclays, where she was group head of strategic policy, to deputy governor for prudential regulation on 1 July 2026, barred from supervisory or enforcement decisions on Barclays for her first six months. No ethics finding is recorded on these moves. The United Kingdom scores 24 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:USA: The US dollar is issued through the Federal Reserve System. Banks that join hold stock in their district's Reserve Bank: Citibank held 42.8 percent of the New York Fed at the end of 2018, JPMorgan Chase 29.5 percent. The Board says the System is not owned by anyone; member banks elect six of each Reserve Bank's nine directors. Of 34 recorded moves between the Fed and private finance, none is an accusation. The Fed's Inspector General found in September 2024 that trades made for Raphael Bostic from 2017 broke ethics rules but no insider trading law, and in January 2024 that Robert Kaplan's 2020 trades looked like acting on confidential policy information, Eric Rosengren having failed to report his. A report of 15 November 2025 found Adriana Kugler's 2024 trades broke Fed rules. Jerome Powell's and Richard Clarida's trades were cleared; Jeffrey Lacker resigned in April 2017 over a 2012 leak, without charges. President Donald Trump has said Powell should resign; the Justice Department subpoenaed the Fed in January 2026; and after he moved to fire Governor Lisa Cook the Supreme Court ruled on 29 June 2026 that she stays. It scores 54 of 100 for exposure to outside influence.
p:VUT: The Reserve Bank of Vanuatu issues the vatu (VUV), held within a band of 2% or less against the Australian dollar. It scores 33 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed. Its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it. Its legal independence scores 0.498 of 1 on the Garriga measure, rank 135 of 191. One case is recorded. A 3 July 1996 Ombudsman report found that governor Samson Ngwele improperly executed ten bank guarantees totalling US$100,000,000, without Board approval and under pressure from Finance Minister Barak Sope, breaching the Reserve Bank Act and the Leadership Code. The guarantees went to Peter Harold Swanson for a 'Trading Programme' that the Ombudsman called a scam.
p:JAM: The Bank of Jamaica issues the Jamaican dollar (JMD), which follows a pre-announced crawling peg against the US dollar, meaning a planned slow drift in the fixed rate. It scores 25 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, less exposed than 80% of the 194 places scored. Its legal independence is 0.661 of 1 on Romelli's rules. Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case is recorded, and it is alleged: governor Derick Latibeaudiere borrowed $51 million from the bank for a house, furnishings and landscaping. At a Public Accounts Committee hearing on 26 May 2009, Auditor General Pamela Monroe Ellis said she had no documents showing the loans were secured and that $25 million of it was still unsecured. The bank's lawyer said $30 million was fully secured.
p:DZA: The Bank of Algeria issues the dinar (DZD), held within a band of 2% or less against the euro. It scores 41 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, more exposed than 83% of the 194 places scored. Its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it. Government pressure was reported in 3 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, including demands to print money. It holds 173.6 tonnes of gold, 33.7% of reserves. It is part-owner of the Bank for International Settlements, which is owned only by central banks. One case is recorded. In the Khalifa Bank case, the Blida criminal court sentenced former governor Abdelwahab Keramane in absentia to 20 years in prison in 2007, and on 7 June 2022 the same court acquitted him. The pages opened do not state the charges.
p:RWA: The National Bank of Rwanda issues the Rwandan franc (RWF), which follows a de facto crawling peg against the US dollar, meaning a slow, managed drift in the rate. It scores 27 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, less exposed than 72% of the 194 places scored. Its legal independence is 0.595 of 1 on Romelli's rules. Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case is recorded: the bank lost Rwf63 million from deposit accounts in early 2014 in a fraud reported to involve staff. The ICT director said suspects manipulated the internal security system. One person was arrested and the file went to the Prosecutor General, while police said the prime suspect was believed to have fled to Uganda. The case is listed as under investigation.
p:CUW: The Central Bank of Curaçao and Sint Maarten issues the Caribbean guilder (XCG), pegged to the US dollar. It scores 50 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, more exposed than 96% of the 194 places scored. Neither independence index codes it. Crane Currency, headquartered in Massachusetts, was contracted to print the new banknotes. One case is recorded. In July 2024 a court found former president Tromp and former deputy director Laurents guilty of document forgery over a backdated 2009 loan agreement under which over $400,000 went to Tromp's pension account. It acquitted them of official bribery and money laundering, including over a $1.5 million 2015 payment from the Venezuelan company Enpiso.
p:BRN: Brunei Darussalam Central Bank issues the Brunei dollar (BND), which operates as a currency board, meaning it is held at a fixed rate to the Singapore dollar. Under a 1967 agreement with Singapore's monetary authority, each side accepts the other's notes and coins at par. The bank scores 46 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, more exposed than 93% of the 194 places scored. Its legal independence is 0.704 of 1 on Romelli's rules. No documented case at the central bank was found, which is not proof none happened. It has one swap line, an agreement to borrow another central bank's currency, through the ASEAN+3 regional arrangement, with a contribution of USD 0.06 billion. Note Printing Australia printed banknotes for it.
p:SAU: The Saudi Central Bank issues the riyal (SAR), held at a fixed rate to the US dollar. It scores 28 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, less exposed than 65% of the 194 places scored. Its legal independence is 0.501 of 1 on Romelli's rules, rank 138 of 155, with a financial independence score of 0. Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. No documented case at the central bank was found, which is not proof none happened. It has one swap line, an agreement to borrow another central bank's currency, with China: CNY 50 billion or SAR 26 billion, signed 20 November 2023 for three years. It is part-owner of the Bank for International Settlements and takes part in the Financial Stability Board. It holds 323.1 tonnes of gold.
p:LCA: The Eastern Caribbean Central Bank (ECCB) issues the EC dollar (XCD) for 8 members, among them Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada and Saint Lucia. The currency is fixed at EC$2.70 = US$1.00 and has been since July 1976; the law requires reserves of at least 60% of currency in circulation. The agreement was signed on 5 July 1983. The bank scores 26 of 100 for St. Lucia, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, less exposed than 75% of the 194 places scored. Its legal independence is 0.549 of 1 on Romelli's rules. Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case is recorded. After the ECCB seized the Stanford-owned Bank of Antigua, the Official Stanford Investors Committee sued it in Dallas in 2013, alleging it misappropriated assets belonging to Stanford's victims and creditors. On 17 August 2018 a US federal judge dismissed the claims in full because the ECCB and Antigua are immune under US foreign sovereign immunity law.

p:TJK: The National Bank of Tajikistan issues the somoni (TJS), held within a band of 2% or less against the US dollar. It has one swap line, an agreement to borrow another central bank's currency, with China: 3 billion yuan, signed 3 September 2015 for three years, with extension possible; whether it is in force is not known. One case is recorded. In March 2008 the IMF Executive Board found that the bank had supplied inaccurate information on the cotton sector, reserves, net domestic assets and credit policy, including reporting reserves of about $450 million when they were roughly one-third of that.
p:ATG: Antigua and Barbuda uses the EC dollar (XCD), issued by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank (ECCB), which sets monetary policy for 8 members. The EC dollar has been fixed at EC$2.70 = US$1.00 since July 1976 (a peg). Its laws score 0.549 of 1 on one independence index and 0.642 on another, where 1 means the bank holds the power; lending to government scores 0.08 on the first. Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters in 2010-2018. In one case, the Official Stanford Investors Committee sued the ECCB in Dallas in 2013, alleging it fraudulently misappropriated assets after it seized the Stanford-owned Bank of Antigua. A US federal judge dismissed the claims in full on 17 August 2018 because the ECCB is immune under US foreign sovereign immunity law. The exposure score is 27 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 fully exposed; the highest part is corruption and secrecy around it, at 53.
p:AIA: Anguilla uses the EC dollar (XCD), issued by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank (ECCB), which sets monetary policy for 8 members. A US federal judge dismissed the claims in full on 17 August 2018 because the ECCB is immune under US foreign sovereign immunity law. The exposure score is 27 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 fully exposed; the highest part is corruption and secrecy around it, at 53.

The EC dollar has been fixed at EC$2.70 = US$1.00 since July 1976 (a peg). Its law scores 0.642 of 1 on one independence index, where 1 means the bank holds the power. Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters in 2010-2018. In one case, the Official Stanford Investors Committee sued the ECCB in Dallas in 2013, alleging it fraudulently misappropriated assets after it seized the Stanford-owned Bank of Antigua. A US federal judge dismissed the claims in full on 17 August 2018 because the ECCB is immune under US foreign sovereign immunity law.
