p:BTN: Bhutan's central bank is the Royal Monetary Authority, which issues the ngultrum and keeps it pegged, or fixed, to the Indian rupee; the rupee circulates in the country as well. One case is recorded. An anonymous informer raised concerns in October 2014 about a former deputy governor, and the final findings of Bhutan's Anti-Corruption Commission for 2014 to 2016 said he allegedly forged official documents, misused power and concealed earnings from World Bank and Asian Development Bank projects. Those allegations are unproven; the commission sent the case to the Office of the Attorney General. A currency swap with India, letting each side borrow up to 100 million US dollars, was signed on 17 March 2016 and expired in March 2019. The bank scores 25 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, less exposed than 82 percent of the 194 places measured.
p:XKX: Kosovo has no currency of its own and uses the euro; its central bank is the Central Bank of the Republic of Kosovo. It used the Deutsche Mark from September 1999 and changed to the euro in 2002, finished on 28 February 2002 in cooperation with the ECB. In July 2010 EU law enforcement officials arrested governor Hashim Rexhepi on suspicion of abusing his position, accepting bribes, tax evasion, trading in influence and money laundering. A Eulex judge threw out all charges on December 12, and in January 2012 Eulex said its prosecutor would take no further action after losing an appeal. He was acquitted. On 16 April 2026 the bank signed an agreement under which the World Bank Treasury's RAMP program will manage a portion of its reserves from 2026. No exposure score is given because too little data exists.
p:PNG: The Bank of Papua New Guinea issues the kina (PGK), run as a de facto crawling peg against the US dollar. Its law scores 0.456 of 1 on one independence index, where 1 means the bank holds the power. According to court documents obtained by OCCRP, the National Fraud and Anti-Corruption Directorate searched the bank's offices in August-September 2023 in a money-laundering investigation into then-acting governor Genia. She obtained a temporary stay that was later dismissed. She was appointed governor in early 2024 and has not been charged. Note Printing Australia prints the bank's banknotes. The exposure score is 36 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 fully exposed; the highest part is corruption and secrecy around it, at 68.
p:MKD: North Macedonia's money is the denar, issued by the National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia and held in practice at a fixed rate to the euro. It scores 24 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it. One case is recorded, running from 2017 to 2020, and it is unproven: an association of depositors of Eurostandard Bank said in a press release that the governor tipped off the finance minister and other large depositors so they could take their money out before the bank was put under administration, and that financial police reports were kept secret so it could keep operating. The association said Finance Minister Nina Angelovska withdrew more than 200,000 euros months before the central bank acted, and that over 60 million euros were lost; no charges and no official finding are reported. The European Central Bank gave the bank a temporary line to borrow euros against collateral from 15 December 2022 to 15 January 2024, which has expired.
p:BLZ: The Central Bank of Belize issues the Belize dollar (BZD), held at a fixed rate to the US dollar (a peg). Its law scores 0.556 of 1 on one independence index, where 1 means the bank holds the power. In August 2021 governor Gustavo Manuel Vasquez lost his post. Prime Minister John Briceño said the board recommended he resign because of "a lot of policy differences". Vasquez wrote that his appointment was terminated on the instructions of the Ministry of Finance, that he faced opposition from it, and that he had tried to restore the bank's integrity and operational autonomy. The exposure score is 32 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 fully exposed; the highest part is corruption and secrecy around it, at 56.
p:GIN: The Central Bank of the Republic of Guinea issues the Guinean franc (GNF). On 23 June 2026 the appeals chamber of Guinea's CRIEF court convicted former governor Bah in absentia of embezzlement of public funds and related offences. It sentenced him to five years, ordered repayment of $10.5 million taken from the central bank's coffers without trace, and imposed a GNF 5 billion fine and confiscation of assets. His defence said the funds were released on instruction. Government pressure was reported in 4 of 37 quarters in 2010-2018, all 4 pressing to cut rates or ease and demanding the bank print money; 2 fell in election periods. Its law scores 0.652 of 1 on one independence index, where 1 means the bank holds the power. The exposure score is 29 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 fully exposed.
p:COM: The Central Bank of the Comoros issues the Comorian franc (KMF), which France guarantees. A cooperation agreement signed on 23 November 1979 bases this on an unlimited French guarantee. The bank must deposit 65% of its foreign exchange reserves with the French Treasury. Under statutes in force since March 2025, France designates two of six Board members, two of four Banking Supervision Committee members and two of four Monetary Policy and Reserve Management Committee members. Its law scores 0.439 of 1 on one independence index and 0.682 on another, where 1 means the bank holds the power. No documented case at the bank was found. The exposure score is 61 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 fully exposed, which ranks 1 of 194; outside influence scores 52 and corruption and secrecy around it 71.
p:TKM: The Central Bank of Turkmenistan issues the manat (TMT). In March 2002 the prosecutor's office accused former central bank chairman Orazov of embezzling $120 million in German and Swiss loans, according to Interfax. On 29 December 2002 the Supreme Court sentenced Orazov in absentia to 25 years over alleged involvement in the 25 November 2002 armed attack on President Niyazov. Its law scores 0.41 of 1 on one independence index and 0.183 on another, where 1 means the bank holds the power; the second ranks 187 of 191. Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters in 2010-2018. The exposure score is 31 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 fully exposed; the highest part is corruption and secrecy around it, at 74.
p:MRT: The Central Bank of Mauritania issues Mauritania's money, the ouguiya. One case is recorded, from 2020 and 2021, and it is still an investigation. In July 2020 police working under the Nouakchott-Ouest prosecutor arrested six people, one of them a bank employee, over foreign currency taken from the central bank. Early reports put the amount at about $1 million and later reports at $2.4 million, plus $500,000 in counterfeit notes. By March 2021 seven people were in pretrial detention, presumed to have taken about $1 million, and supporters held a sit-in demanding a quick trial. The reports reviewed show no trial or verdict. The bank scores 28 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and its weakest side is corruption in the country and money-laundering risk in its banks.
p:ARE: The Central Bank of the United Arab Emirates issues the dirham and holds it at a fixed rate against the US dollar, an arrangement called a peg. No case at the bank is documented, and government pressure was reported in none of the 37 quarters surveyed between 2010 and 2018. Its law gives it middling independence, 0.685 of 1 on one index and 0.457 on another, where 1 means the bank holds the power. It is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, and it holds nine swap lines, agreements to borrow another central bank's currency. It held 297.8 billion US dollars of assets at the end of 2025 and 74.5 tonnes of gold. It scores 27 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, the highest part being corruption and secrecy around it at 57.
p:PAN: Panama has no central bank. Banco Nacional de Panamá is a state commercial bank, and the country uses the US dollar. The IMF lists Panama with Ecuador, El Salvador, the Marshall Islands, Micronesia, Palau and Timor-Leste as having no separate legal tender, with the US dollar as anchor. The US dollar is 89.08% of world currency trading, 56.7% of foreign reserves and 50.1% of Swift payments, and 16 places use it. No documented case at a central bank was found. The country has had 1 systemic banking crisis since 1970, and its financial secrecy score is 78.4 of 100. The exposure score is 53 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 fully exposed, which ranks 6 of 194; corruption and secrecy around it scores 67 and outside influence 39.
p:BDI: The Bank of the Republic of Burundi is the central bank of Burundi, which uses the Burundian franc. One case is recorded. In October 2023 the Ministry of Justice said that the dismissed governor, Dieudonné Murengerantwari, was being prosecuted for passive corruption (taking bribes), money laundering, misappropriation of public property and undermining the national economy. The prosecutor called this description of the facts provisional, and the governor was being questioned at the time of the report. He is charged, and nothing is reported as proven. The bank scores 32 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and its weakest side is corruption in the country.
p:ARM: The Central Bank of Armenia is the central bank of Armenia, which uses the dram. No cases or pressure on the bank are recorded, and government pressure was reported in none of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018. The bank rejoined the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, a program that serves nearly 100 members and manages over $25 billion for them. Membership alone does not show that the bank hands over its assets to be managed. It has a swap line with China, an agreement to lend each other currency, for 77 billion drams and one billion yuan, dated March 2015; whether it is still in force is not known. The dram is kept on a crawling peg against the US dollar. The bank scores 20 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, which is less exposed than most places measured.
p:CPV: The Bank of Cape Verde issues the escudo (CVE), which Portugal backs under a cooperation agreement signed on 13 March 1998. The currency is pegged at CVE 110.265 per euro. The Portuguese Treasury provides a short-term credit facility of EUR 27.5 million, expandable to EUR 45 million, with drawdowns capped at EUR 5 million; Cabo Verde must transfer reserves equal to 35% of the amount requested. Banco de Portugal states the facility creates no obligation for it or any Eurosystem institution to intervene. Its law scores 0.518 of 1 on one independence index, where 1 means the bank holds the power. No documented case at the bank was found. The exposure score is 47 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 fully exposed, which ranks 11 of 194; outside influence is the highest part, at 49.
p:BRB: The Central Bank of Barbados issues the Barbados dollar (BBD), run as a de facto peg to the US dollar. Its law scores 0.715 of 1 on one independence index, where 1 means the bank holds the power. In 2017 Finance Minister Chris Sinckler fired Governor Delisle Worrell. The government's stated reason was that the board objected to his reported high-handed manner. Some observers believed the reason was his refusal to keep financing the government with new money: his January letter said the government must stop taking new money from the bank to pay its bills. The Appeals Court upheld the minister's right. Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters in 2010-2018. The exposure score is 28 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 fully exposed.
p:SDN: The Central Bank of Sudan issues the Sudanese pound (SDG). In October 2025 Sovereignty Council head Abdel Fattah al-Burhan dismissed governor Burai Al-Siddiq Ali Ahmed after a dispute over gold purchase and export rules and appointed Amna Mirghani Hassan El Toum. Deputy governor Mohamed Osman Ahmed Mohamed Khair was dismissed less than two weeks later. Government pressure was reported in 2 of 37 quarters in 2010-2018, both pressing to cut rates or ease and demanding the bank print money. Its law scores 0.333 of 1 on one independence index, where 1 means the bank holds the power; this ranks 172 of 191. The exposure score is 43 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 fully exposed; corruption and secrecy around it scores 85.
p:TTO: The Central Bank of Trinidad and Tobago issues the Trinidad and Tobago dollar, which it holds close to the US dollar. It scores 30 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and no government pressure was reported between 2010 and 2018. Both of its records concern the collapse of CL Financial and the Hindu Credit Union. The commission of enquiry into that collapse, commissioned in November 2010 under sole commissioner Sir Anthony Colman, found the bank's powers to regulate insurers 'fundamentally deficient' because of the narrow scope of the Insurance Act, said the Inspector of financial institutions used the limited tools available but that Clico and CL Financial management largely ignored them, and blamed no named bank official. On 6 December 2012 Queen's Counsel Peter Carter put it to former governor Ewart Williams at the enquiry that intervening in 2006 would have kept over 10 billion Trinidad and Tobago dollars from being at risk; Williams said the bank held off to avoid a run on CLICO and intervened in 2009. That was cross-examination, not a finding.
p:QAT: The Qatar Central Bank issues the riyal (QAR), held at a fixed rate to the US dollar (a peg). Its law scores 0.607 of 1 on one independence index and 0.586 on another, where 1 means the bank holds the power. Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters in 2010-2018, and no documented case at the bank was found. It has 4 swap lines, which are agreements to borrow another central bank's currency. They include CNY 35 billion with China, with a renewal agreement dated 14 October 2026, and USD 15 billion equivalent in lira and riyal with Türkiye, amended in 2020, whose current status is not confirmed. It holds 116.2 tonnes of gold, 26.8% of reserves. The exposure score is 28 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 fully exposed.
p:SLV: El Salvador's central bank is the Central Reserve Bank of El Salvador, and the country's currency is listed as both SVC and the US dollar. The IMF's 2023 classification lists El Salvador among places with no separate legal tender, using the US dollar as anchor. Its overall exposure score is 37 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; that is more exposed than 76% of the 194 places with a figure. The weakest side is corruption and secrecy around the bank (62), with a Corruption Perceptions Index score of 32 of 100. Written independence from government scores 0.789 of 1 (rank 47 of 191). Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. No documented case at the central bank was found, which does not prove none happened. The US dollar is used in 16 places and makes up 89.08% of world currency trading.
p:HND: The Central Bank of Honduras issues the currency HNL, held at a crawling peg measured against the US dollar as of December 2025; a peg means holding the currency at a set rate to another currency. Its exposure score is 27 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; the weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it (67), with a Corruption Perceptions Index score of 22 of 100. Written independence from government scores 0.671 of 1 (rank 72 of 191), and government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. On 3 June 2026 Honduran prosecutors charged 11 current and former employees, two of them serving managers, with 100 counts of negligent embezzlement over a scheme that allegedly removed public funds from the bank over several years. They were arrested after the court admitted the case. The charges are unproven.
p:STP: The Central Bank of São Tomé and Príncipe issues the dobra, which is pegged to the euro. It scores 28 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, which leaves it less exposed than most of the places measured, and its weak point is corruption and secrecy around it, chiefly money-laundering risk in its banks. One episode is on record. In June 2006 the cabinet dismissed the governor, Maria do Carmo Silveira, a former prime minister, along with her team, saying it had found irregularities in the construction of the bank's new building, a project valued at 8 million US dollars. What those irregularities were was not set out, and the claim is unproven. The country has had two systemic banking crises since 1970.
p:BHR: The Central Bank of Bahrain, created in 1973, issues the Bahraini Dinar (BHD), held at a peg to the US dollar as of December 2025. Its exposure score is 28 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed. The weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it (56): the country's laws hide who owns money, and financial secrecy scores 69 of 100. Written independence from government scores 0.515 of 1 on one index (rank 135 of 155) and 0.433 on another (rank 156 of 191). Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, and no documented case at the bank was found. A swap line, which is an agreement to borrow another central bank's currency, runs both ways with the United Arab Emirates: BHD 2 billion (AED 20 billion), signed 8 April 2026, for up to 5 years.
p:TLS: Timor-Leste has a Central Bank of Timor-Leste, created in 2001, and uses the US dollar as its currency. The IMF's 2023 classification lists it among places with no separate legal tender, with the dollar as anchor. Its exposure score is 49 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; that is more exposed than 95% of 194 places, with outside influence scoring 41. Written independence from government scores 0.777 of 1 (rank 50 of 191). The weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it (57), with a Corruption Perceptions Index score of 44 of 100. No documented case at the central bank was found, which does not prove none happened. The US dollar is used in 16 places and makes up 89.08% of world currency trading.
p:GUY: The Bank of Guyana issues the currency GYD, held at a de facto peg to the US dollar as of December 2025; a peg means holding the currency at a fixed rate to another. Its exposure score is 29 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed. The weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it (56), with a Corruption Perceptions Index score of 40 of 100. Written independence from government scores 0.609 of 1 (rank 93 of 191), and government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. No documented case at the bank was found. Crane Currency, a banknote maker, is listed as having supplied banknotes, banknote paper and anti-counterfeiting features for the bank; the source is a client list in a third-party announcement, not a contract notice.
p:AND: Andorra has no central bank; the Andorran Financial Authority oversees its finances, and the country uses the euro. Under its monetary agreement with the EU, Andorra may issue its own euro coins from July 2013. The IMF's 2023 classification lists Andorra and San Marino as having no separate legal tender, with the euro as anchor. Little else is scored: no overall exposure score exists, and independence and public transparency are not rated. Money-laundering risk is 3.48 of 10 (rank 171 of 177, where 1 is riskiest), and financial secrecy is 54.4 of 100. No documented case was found. The European Central Bank ran a temporary repo line, a lending arrangement, with Andorra from 15 December 2022 to 15 January 2024; it has expired.
p:UZB: The Central Bank of Uzbekistan, created in 1991, issues the currency UZS, held at a de facto crawling peg to the US dollar as of December 2025. Its exposure score is 32 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; outside influence scores 3 and corruption and secrecy around the bank 60. Written independence from government scores 0.862 of 1 on one index (rank 26 of 155) and 0.604 on another (rank 95 of 191). Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, and no documented case at the bank was found. Gold holdings are 431.7 tonnes, 87.5% of reserves. A swap line, an agreement to borrow another central bank's currency, with China was set at RMB 0.7 billion in April 2011; whether it is in force is not known.
p:SWZ: The Central Bank of Eswatini, set up in 1974, issues the country's currency, fixed at par to the South African rand under the Common Monetary Area. It scores 34 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Two findings cover one licensing fight. In 2017 a bank evaluations team recommended rejecting Farmers Bank's application for a commercial banking licence, and it was turned down late that year. Governor Majozi Sithole said a royal command required him to attend a meeting about the venture on 14 July 2017, and in May 2018 finance minister Martin Dlamini said King Mswati III had ordered an investigation into the bank's reluctance to license it. A conditional licence followed in September 2018 after a royal command. The bank revoked it on 5 October 2020 because the source of the seed capital was unexplained; commerce minister Manqoba Khumalo ruled that December that Farmers Bank should keep it, and the bank reinstated it in January 2021 while objecting to procedural improprieties. A 2022 report by Kroll, commissioned by the bank, said third parties outside it had likely intervened and instructed it to proceed, and that 89 million rand of seed capital had gone from 2019 into silver bullion the bank could not verify existed.
p:HTI: The Bank of the Republic of Haiti, created in 1979, issues the currency HTG, held at a de facto peg to the US dollar as of December 2025; the dollar is also listed as a currency there. Its exposure score is 49 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; that is more exposed than 95% of 194 places. Corruption and secrecy around it scores 82, with a Corruption Perceptions Index score of 16 of 100 and money-laundering risk of 8.12 of 10 (rank 2 of 177, where 1 is riskiest). Written independence from government scores 0.366 of 1 on one index (rank 151 of 155) and 0.376 on another (rank 165 of 191). Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, and no documented case at the bank was found.
p:CRI: The Central Bank of Costa Rica issues the currency CRC, kept within a moving band of plus or minus 2% against the US dollar as of December 2025. Its exposure score is 28 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; outside influence scores only 5. Written independence from government is high: 0.826 of 1 on one index (rank 41 of 155) and 0.734 on another (rank 55 of 191). Government pressure was reported in 1 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, and that pressure was a threat to change the law. No documented case at the bank was found, which does not prove none happened. The country has had 2 systemic banking crises since 1970.
p:JOR: The Central Bank of Jordan issues the Jordanian dinar and holds it at a fixed rate against the US dollar, an arrangement called a peg. It scores 29 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 fully exposed. Its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, at 57, mainly because the country's laws hide who owns money: it scores 75.7 of 100 for financial secrecy. Written independence from government scores 0.659 of 1 on one index and 0.759 on another. No case at the bank is documented, and no government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters surveyed from 2010 to 2018. In September 2003 members of Jordan's parliament signed a petition urging Prime Minister Ali Abulragheb to remove governor Umayya Touqan, after Touqan froze all bank accounts belonging to six leaders of Hamas. Whether the government acted on it is not known. The bank holds 78.7 tonnes of gold.
p:SLB: The Central Bank of Solomon Islands, created in 1976, issues the currency SBD, held at a crawling peg to the US dollar as of December 2025. Its exposure score is 31 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed. Written independence from government scores 0.745 of 1 (rank 53 of 191). One case is recorded: a former central bank employee, Bobongi, was convicted on 39 counts of money laundering and two counts of larceny and embezzlement for stealing more than $1.7 million in old banknotes in 2007-2009 while the bank was destroying them, and was sentenced to nine years. Money-laundering risk in the country is 6.31 of 10 (rank 34 of 177, where 1 is riskiest).
p:ABW: The Central Bank of Aruba, created in 1986, issues the currency AWG, held at a peg to the US dollar as of December 2025. Its exposure score is 29 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed. The weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it (51): financial secrecy scores 67.3 of 100. Written independence from government scores 0.446 of 1 (rank 149 of 191), with the governor and policy-making measures both at 0. No documented case at the bank was found. Crane Currency, a banknote maker, is listed as having supplied Aruba's new banknotes in 2019; the source is a client list in a third-party announcement, not a contract notice. Gold holdings are 3.1 tonnes, 18.9% of reserves.
p:MAC: The Monetary Authority of Macao issues the currency MOP, held at a peg to the US dollar as of December 2025. Its exposure score is 31 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed. Written independence from government is low: 0.271 of 1, the lowest rank of 155, with lending to government scored 0. It scores 6.5 of 15 on public transparency (rank 60 of 112). No documented case at the authority was found. It has two swap lines with China, which are agreements to borrow another central bank's currency. One, signed 5 December 2025, runs both ways for CNY 50 billion (MOP 57 billion) with no end date. An earlier line of RMB 30 billion dates from December 2019; whether it is in force is not known.
p:OMN: The Central Bank of Oman, created in 1974, issues the currency OMR, held at a peg to the US dollar as of December 2025; a peg means holding the currency at a fixed rate to another. Its exposure score is 27 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed. The weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it (53): financial secrecy scores 72.4 of 100. Written independence from government scores 0.618 of 1 on one index (rank 109 of 155) and 0.46 on another (rank 145 of 191). Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, and no documented case at the bank was found. Gold holdings are 6.7 tonnes, 3.6% of reserves.
p:SYC: The Central Bank of Seychelles, created in 1983, issues the currency SCR, kept within a moving band of plus or minus 2% against the US dollar as of December 2025. Its exposure score is 26 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; that is less exposed than 77% of 194 places. Corruption and secrecy around it scores 49, with a Corruption Perceptions Index score of 68 of 100 and financial secrecy of 71.9 of 100. Written independence from government scores 0.594 of 1 on one index (rank 116 of 155) and 0.582 on another (rank 106 of 191). No documented case at the bank was found, which does not prove none happened.
p:BHS: The Central Bank of the Bahamas issues the currency BSD, held at a peg to the US dollar as of December 2025. Its exposure score is 26 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed. The weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it (53): financial secrecy scores 75.4 of 100 (rank 32 of 141), and the Corruption Perceptions Index score is 64 of 100. Written independence from government scores 0.719 of 1 on one index (rank 77 of 155) and 0.727 on another (rank 56 of 191). Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, and no documented case at the bank was found.
p:DOM: The Dominican Republic's money is the peso, issued by the Central Bank of the Dominican Republic and held within a crawling band of 2 per cent or less against the US dollar as of December 2025. The bank scores 22 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it. One case is recorded and the charges are unproven: the Directorate for the Prosecution of Administrative Corruption took former governor Jose Lois Malkun, former deputy governor Felix Calvo, former administrative director Cesar Apolinar Veloz and former legal counsel Manuel Rubio Cristoforis to court on charges including breach of trust and criminal association, over the disappearance of 18 promissory notes worth 10,663 million Dominican pesos said to have been handed fraudulently to the former banker Manuel Arturo Pellerano. The central bank neither filed a complaint nor joined the case as a civil party, and a Monetary Board resolution said its authorities were negotiating the return of the notes with Pellerano.
p:URY: Uruguay's money is the peso, issued by the Central Bank of Uruguay and held within a moving band of 2 per cent or less against the US dollar as of December 2025. The bank scores 25 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, though the country scores 73 of 100 on the Corruption Perceptions Index. One case is recorded, from 2017, and it was dismissed: prosecutor Rodrigo Morosoli, investigating the Cambio Nelson fraud at a currency exchange house, asked for the formal indictment of Humberto Capote, a former president of the bank, for taking part in a continuing crime of misappropriation. Judge Marcelo Souto freed Capote at first instance, finding the evidence insufficient to prosecute him, and the prosecutor appealed in April 2017. No government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters surveyed from 2010 to 2018.
p:TWN: The Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan) issues the New Taiwan dollar (TWD). Its exposure score is 31 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed. n:José Filomeno dos Santos: José Filomeno dos Santos is a person from Angola, tied to the National Bank of Angola through a court case. n:International Monetary Fund: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) is an international lender based in Washington, United States, tied to 16 central banks and one other party. Its former staff have gone on to lead central banks. Kamau Thugge went from IMF staff to governor of the Central Bank of Kenya, and Reza Baqir from IMF staff to governor of the State Bank of Pakistan. Agustín Carstens went from IMF deputy managing director to governor of the Bank of Mexico, and Raghuram Rajan from IMF chief economist to governor of the Reserve Bank of India. Ahsan H Mansur went from IMF staff to governor of Bangladesh Bank. These are career moves, not accusations. The IMF also appears in cases. In May 2023 Argentina's central bank used 99.2% of a transfer limit it had agreed with the IMF. In December 2021 Malawi police arrested Kabambe and Mwanamvekha, saying they falsified figures to make the IMF believe Malawi met loan conditions. In March 2008 the IMF Executive Board found that the National Bank of Tajikistan had supplied inaccurate information, including reporting reserves of about $450 million when they were roughly one-third of that, and Tajikistan was required to repay $47.4 million. The IMF also sits on the Financial Stability Board.
n:Securency: Securency is a banknote-material company in Melbourne, Australia, tied to six central banks. It was a 50-50 joint venture of the Reserve Bank of Australia and Innovia, and it is now called CCL Secure. It supplies the polymer plastic used for the Bank of Canada's banknotes that began circulating in 2011. In October 2011 Securency and Note Printing Australia pleaded guilty in the Supreme Court of Victoria to conspiring to give benefits to foreign officials to win banknote business with the note-issuing authorities of Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam and Nepal. Securency paid a penalty of A$19,809,772. Its former chief financial officer received a suspended six-month sentence for false accounting in 2012, and its agent Radius Christanto a suspended two-year sentence in 2013. The officials who received the benefits are not named. In Nigeria, the anti-corruption agency EFCC questioned former governor Soludo around 2013 in a probe into whether Securency bribed Central Bank of Nigeria officials to win a contract to print polymer notes between 2006 and 2008. No outcome is given.
n:Note Printing Australia: Note Printing Australia (NPA) is a banknote printer in Melbourne, Australia, wholly owned by the Reserve Bank of Australia and tied to nine central banks. In 2006/07 it produced 245 million notes for the Reserve Bank of Australia and filled export orders for the central banks of Chile, Malaysia, Papua New Guinea, Brunei, Singapore and New Zealand. In October 2011 NPA and Securency pleaded guilty in the Supreme Court of Victoria to conspiring to give benefits to foreign officials to win banknote business in Indonesia, Malaysia and Nepal. NPA paid a penalty of A$1,856,710. The officials are not named. Separately, a former Bank Negara Malaysia official, Mohamad Daud, was charged in July 2011 with taking two bribes of RM50,000 each in 2004-2005, linked to a RM95 million polymer note contract won by NPA. The Shah Alam Sessions Court acquitted him on 6 December 2015 without calling his defence, and the Attorney-General withdrew the appeal in February 2016.

n:Radius Christanto: Radius Christanto is a person based in Indonesia, tied to the Reserve Bank of Australia. He was an agent for Securency, a banknote-material company part-owned by that bank. In October 2011 Securency and Note Printing Australia pleaded guilty to conspiring to bribe foreign officials to win banknote business in Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam and Nepal. Christanto received a suspended two-year sentence in 2013, meaning he was not jailed unless he broke its conditions.
n:Bank Indonesia: Bank Indonesia is the central bank of Indonesia, based in Jakarta, tied to the Reserve Bank of Australia. In October 2011 two Reserve Bank of Australia subsidiaries, Securency and Note Printing Australia, pleaded guilty in the Supreme Court of Victoria to conspiring to give benefits to foreign officials to win banknote business with Indonesia's note-issuing authority between 1999 and 2001. The officials are not named. The companies paid penalties of A$19.8 million and A$1.86 million, and agent Radius Christanto received a suspended two-year sentence in 2013.
n:Bank Negara Malaysia: Bank Negara Malaysia is the central bank of Malaysia, based in Kuala Lumpur, tied to the Reserve Bank of Australia. In October 2011 two Reserve Bank of Australia subsidiaries, Securency and Note Printing Australia, pleaded guilty in the Supreme Court of Victoria to conspiring to give benefits to foreign officials to win banknote business with Malaysia's note-issuing authority between 2001 and 2003. They paid penalties of A$19.8 million and A$1.86 million. Separately, former Bank Negara official Mohamad Daud was charged in July 2011 with taking two RM50,000 bribes in 2004-2005, linked to a RM95 million polymer note contract. The Shah Alam Sessions Court acquitted him on 6 December 2015, and the Attorney-General withdrew the appeal in February 2016.
n:State Bank of Vietnam: The State Bank of Vietnam is the central bank of Vietnam, based in Hanoi, tied to the Reserve Bank of Australia. In October 2011 Securency, a Reserve Bank of Australia joint venture, pleaded guilty in the Supreme Court of Victoria to conspiring to give benefits to foreign officials to win banknote business with Vietnam's note-issuing authority between 2001 and 2004. The officials are not named. Securency paid a penalty of A$19,809,772, and its former chief financial officer received a suspended six-month sentence in 2012 for false accounting.
n:Nepal Rastra Bank: Nepal Rastra Bank is the central bank of Nepal, based in Kathmandu, tied to the Reserve Bank of Australia. In October 2011 Note Printing Australia, a Reserve Bank of Australia subsidiary, pleaded guilty in the Supreme Court of Victoria to conspiring to give benefits to foreign officials to win banknote business with Nepal's note-issuing authority between 2000 and 2002. The officials are not named. The company paid a penalty of A$1,856,710. Agent Radius Christanto received a suspended two-year sentence in 2013 in the wider case.
n:OeBS: OeBS is a banknote printing company in Vienna, Austria, owned by the Oesterreichische Nationalbank, Austria's central bank, and tied to three central banks. A Vienna court found that OeBS overcharged the Central Bank of Azerbaijan by 20% and the Central Bank of Syria by 14% on banknote contracts, and that the extra money returned as kickbacks to local decision makers. About 14 million euros was paid. Seven defendants were convicted in October 2014. After a retrial ordered by the Supreme Court, the Vienna court in February 2018 gave Wolf and Miller 18-month suspended sentences and Meyer 21 months suspended. Former Nationalbank deputy governor Duchatczek was acquitted. No Azerbaijani or Syrian official was named or tried.
n:Michael Wolf: Michael Wolf is a person based in Vienna, Austria, and a former manager of OeBS, the banknote printing subsidiary of the Oesterreichische Nationalbank. Seven defendants were convicted in October 2014. After a retrial ordered by the Supreme Court, the Vienna court in February 2018 gave Wolf an 18-month suspended sentence.

n:Baku court: The Baku court is a court in Baku, Azerbaijan, tied to the Central Bank of Azerbaijan. In September 2009 it sentenced six former central bank officers for abuse of power and embezzlement of 1.4 million Azerbaijani manat from the bank between 2003 and 2008. Sentences ranged from a two-year suspended term to eight years.
n:Anti-Corruption Commission (Bangladesh: The Anti-Corruption Commission is a government agency in Dhaka, Bangladesh, tied to Bangladesh Bank, the central bank. On 14 January 2025 it arrested former deputy governor SK Sur in a case about failing to submit an asset statement. It had opened an investigation into him in 2022 over allegations that, while at the central bank, he helped and benefited from a loan scam run by PK Halder. In June 2025 it opened an investigation into former governor Atiur Rahman over alleged abuse of power, policies favouring loan defaulters, and enabling frauds including the Hallmark and S Alam Group scandals and the 2016 reserve heist. It had prosecuted Atiur in February 2025 over the AnonTex loan scam. These matters are allegations, and no outcome is given.
n:PK Halder: PK Halder is a person tied to Bangladesh Bank, with his marker placed at Bangladesh as a whole. He is named as the person who ran a loan scam. In 2022 Bangladesh's Anti-Corruption Commission opened an investigation into former Bangladesh Bank deputy governor SK Sur over allegations that he facilitated and benefited from that scam while at the central bank. The commission arrested Sur on 14 January 2025 in a separate case about failing to submit an asset statement. The allegations against Sur are unproven.
n:Hallmark Group: Hallmark Group is a company in Dhaka, Bangladesh, tied to Bangladesh Bank, the central bank. The commission is examining alleged abuse of power and policies favouring loan defaulters that enabled such frauds. It sought central bank records on two other former governors and several deputy governors. This is an investigation, and the allegations are unproven.

n:AnonTex Group: AnonTex Group is a company in Dhaka, Bangladesh, tied to Bangladesh Bank, the central bank. In June 2025 the commission also opened a wider investigation into him over alleged abuse of power and policies favouring loan defaulters. n:Federal Reserve Bank of New York: The Federal Reserve Bank of New York is a bank in New York, United States, that holds accounts for other central banks, and it is tied to two of them. Attackers used Bangladesh Bank's SWIFT access (the messaging network banks use to move money) on the night of 4 February 2016 to steal reserves from its account there. The amount was $101 million according to The Daily Star and $81 million according to Prothom Alo. A government inquiry's final report of 30 May 2016 hinted at involvement of central bank officials. It was never published, and no one was punished as of 2019. The New York Fed also held much of the nearly $9.5 billion of Da Afghanistan Bank assets that the United States froze after the Taliban takeover in August 2021.
n:Government of Bangladesh: The Government of Bangladesh, based in Dhaka, is tied to Bangladesh Bank, the central bank. n:Bulgarian prosecutors: Bulgarian prosecutors are an agency based in Sofia, Bulgaria. They charged two former deputy governors of the Bulgarian National Bank, the country's central bank, who had been in charge of supervision. The charge was failing to take legally required measures against Corporate Commercial Bank (Corpbank) from February 2010, allegedly to benefit its shareholders. Gounev was charged in June 2014 and removed from office by court order in December 2014. Simeonov was charged about ten months later. Corpbank collapsed in June 2014, and its majority owner was accused of embezzling 206 million leva. These are charges and allegations, and no outcome is given.
n:Corporate Commercial Bank: Corporate Commercial Bank, called Corpbank, is a bank based in Sofia, Bulgaria. Prosecutors charged two former deputy governors in charge of supervision with failing to take legally required measures against Corpbank from February 2010, allegedly to benefit its shareholders. Gounev was charged in June 2014 and removed from office by court order in December 2014. Simeonov was charged about ten months later. Corpbank collapsed in June 2014, and its majority owner was accused of embezzling 206 million leva. The charges and accusations are unproven.
n:Banco Mercantil Santa Cruz: Banco Mercantil Santa Cruz is a bank based in La Paz, Bolivia. It is tied to the Central Bank of Bolivia as one of the local financial entities that dealt with it. On 28 April 2026 Bolivian authorities detained the former central bank president and three other former senior officials over seven debt-swap operations with local financial entities in June and July 2024. The swaps were made at inflated prices and cost the state 142.3 million dollars. The vice minister of transparency said price records were later altered on internal email instructions to hide the overvaluation. The suspects deny wrongdoing, and seven people are under investigation, so nothing is proven.

n:BTG Pactual: BTG Pactual is a bank based in São Paulo, Brazil, tied to two central banks and one other party. On 3 October 2019 Brazil's Federal Police and the São Paulo federal prosecutors launched Operation Estrela Cadente. It looks into leaks from the Central Bank of Brazil of Copom interest-rate decisions in 2010, 2011 and 2012, allegedly to benefit a BTG Pactual fund. They are investigating passive and active corruption, insider information and money laundering. Details remained under court seal, and the allegations are unproven. BTG Pactual also has a link to people: Guillermo Ortiz went from governor of the Bank of Mexico to chairman of BTG Pactual Mexico. He also represents BTG Pactual in the Group of Thirty, a forum where central bankers and private-sector figures sit together.
n:Federal Police of Brazil: The Federal Police of Brazil is an agency based in Brasília. The inquiry concerns leaks of Copom interest-rate decisions in 2010, 2011 and 2012 to benefit a fund of the bank BTG Pactual.
