n:Kashya Hildebrand: Kashya Hildebrand is a person, placed on the map at Switzerland as a whole. Hildebrand is named in a documented case involving the Swiss National Bank, the country's central bank. In that case, Hildebrand resigned on 9 January 2012 after reports that dollar trades made in 2011 from a joint account with his wife earned tens of thousands of dollars while the bank was acting to weaken the franc. He said the trades broke no rules but that he could not prove he was unaware of them. He donated the profits to charity.
n:Huanggang Intermediate People's Court: The Huanggang Intermediate People's Court is a court in Huanggang, China. In October 2024 it sentenced Fan Yifei, a former deputy governor of the People's Bank of China, the country's central bank, to death with a two-year reprieve. The sentence is to be commuted to life without parole. The court found he had accepted property worth more than 386 million yuan by taking advantage of his posts at the central bank and other institutions, including China Construction Bank.
n:China Construction Bank: China Construction Bank is a bank based in Beijing, China. It is named in a documented case involving the People's Bank of China, the country's central bank. In October 2024 the Huanggang Intermediate People's Court sentenced Fan Yifei, a former deputy governor of the central bank, to death with a two-year reprieve, to be commuted to life without parole. The court found he accepted property worth more than 386 million yuan by taking advantage of his posts at the central bank and other institutions, including China Construction Bank.
n:Mfoundi court: The Mfoundi court is a court in Yaoundé, Cameroon. It heard a case about the Bank of Central African States (BEAC), the central bank shared by several Central African countries. A November 2009 internal BEAC report found about 20 billion CFA francs had been diverted from the bank's Paris office to 139 beneficiaries between 2004 and 2008. Another account of the report, published in late October 2009, put the loss at about 25 million euros and said internal controls were far below international standards. It said alarming reports reached the governor but no firm action followed. Jean-Pierre Oyiba, chief of staff to Gabon's president, resigned on 9 November 2009 after the report said he received about 100,000 euros, which he denies. On 28 September 2012 the court sentenced Kemadjou to life imprisonment and ordered him to pay BEAC 26.4 billion CFA francs.
n:Enpiso: Enpiso is a company in Venezuela; the map marks the country, not its office. It is tied to the Central Bank of Curaçao and Sint Maarten through a 2015 payment of 1.5 million dollars that prosecutors linked to talks about taking over Girobank. In July 2024 a court tried former central bank president Tromp and former deputy director Laurents. It found them guilty of document forgery over a backdated 2009 loan agreement, under which over 400,000 dollars went to Tromp's pension account. It acquitted them of official bribery and money laundering, which included the Enpiso payment.
n:Girobank: Girobank is a bank based in Willemstad, Curaçao. It is named in a documented case involving the Central Bank of Curaçao and Sint Maarten. Prosecutors linked a 1.5 million dollar payment in 2015 from the Venezuelan company Enpiso to Girobank takeover talks. In July 2024 a court found former central bank president Tromp and former deputy director Laurents guilty of document forgery over a backdated 2009 loan agreement, under which over 400,000 dollars went to Tromp's pension account. It acquitted them of official bribery and money laundering, which included the Enpiso payment.
n:Curaçao court: The Curaçao court is a court in Willemstad, Curaçao. In July 2024 it found former president Tromp and former deputy director Laurents of the Central Bank of Curaçao and Sint Maarten guilty of document forgery. The forgery concerned a backdated 2009 loan agreement under which over 400,000 dollars went to Tromp's pension account. The court acquitted both of official bribery and money laundering, including over a 1.5 million dollar payment in 2015 from the Venezuelan company Enpiso, which prosecutors linked to takeover talks for Girobank.
n:Dresdner Bank: Dresdner Bank is a bank based in Frankfurt, Germany. It is tied to the Deutsche Bundesbank, Germany's central bank. Welteke, the Bundesbank's chief, resigned on 16 April 2004 after criticism for accepting a free New Year stay at Berlin's Hotel Adlon, paid for by a commercial bank two years earlier. The Bundesbank oversees commercial banks. Prosecutors and the Bundesbank had opened inquiries.
n:Hotel Adlon: Hotel Adlon is a hotel company based in Berlin, Germany. It is named in a documented case involving the Deutsche Bundesbank, Germany's central bank. Welteke, the Bundesbank's chief, accepted a free New Year stay at the Hotel Adlon, paid for by a commercial bank two years earlier. The Bundesbank oversees commercial banks. After criticism, and with prosecutors and the Bundesbank having opened inquiries, Welteke resigned on 16 April 2004.
n:German prosecutors: German prosecutors are an agency; the map marks Germany as a whole. They opened an inquiry involving the Deutsche Bundesbank, Germany's central bank. The matter concerned Welteke, the Bundesbank's chief, who accepted a free New Year stay at Berlin's Hotel Adlon, paid for by a commercial bank two years earlier. The Bundesbank oversees commercial banks and also opened its own inquiry. Welteke resigned on 16 April 2004 after criticism.
n:European Ombudsman: The European Ombudsman is an international body based in Strasbourg, France, that examines complaints about European Union institutions. It investigated the European Central Bank. In case 1697/2016/ANA it found maladministration. In January 2018 it recommended that Mario Draghi suspend his membership of the Group of Thirty, a forum where central bankers and private-sector figures sit together, saying the membership was not in keeping with the ECB's independence. The ECB declined, and Draghi did not suspend his membership.
n:Group of Thirty: The Group of Thirty is an organization based in Washington, United States, where current and former central bankers sit alongside private-sector members. It is tied to 20 central banks and 22 other parties. Members tied to central banks include Tharman Shanmugaratnam (Singapore), Raghuram Rajan (chair, formerly Reserve Bank of India), Jean-Claude Trichet and Mario Draghi (European Central Bank), Mervyn King and Andrew Bailey (Bank of England), and Guillermo Ortiz and Agustín Carstens (Bank of Mexico). Private-sector members include Jane Fraser of Citi, Philipp Hildebrand of BlackRock, Gail Kelly of UBS, Maria Ramos of Standard Chartered and Guillermo Ortiz of BTG Pactual. In case 1697/2016/ANA the European Ombudsman found maladministration and in January 2018 recommended that Draghi suspend his membership, saying it was not in keeping with the ECB's independence. The ECB declined, and Draghi did not suspend it.
n:Serious Fraud Office: The Serious Fraud Office is an agency based in London, United Kingdom, tied to two central banks. The Bank of England referred material about its 2007-2008 liquidity auctions to it. The office opened an investigation in 2015 and closed it in June 2017, concluding there was no evidence of criminality. For the Bank of South Sudan, a UN Human Rights Council commission report said De La Rue transferred about 1.4 million dollars to an Equity Bank account in Nairobi held by a Bank of South Sudan consultant between 2016 and September 2017. The banknote contract was worth about 144 million dollars, and the report noted suspected corruption. The office closed its own investigation in June 2020 without charges.
n:House of Commons Treasury Committee: The House of Commons Treasury Committee is a government body based in London, United Kingdom. It examined the Bank of England, the country's central bank. It published a report finding that Hogg, a Bank of England deputy, had failed on multiple occasions since joining the Bank in 2013 to declare her brother's role as director of group strategy at Barclays. The report called this a very serious breach. She said she had also unintentionally misled the committee. Hogg resigned on 14 March 2017.
n:Barclays: Barclays is a bank based in London, United Kingdom, tied to two central banks. David Roberts, Chair of the Bank of England's Court, previously held executive and chair roles at Barclays and other firms. Lord Jitesh Gadhia, a non-executive director of the Court, came from investment banking including Barclays Capital. Katharine Braddick, Deputy Governor for Prudential Regulation from 1 July 2026, was Barclays group head of strategic policy. Barclays also paid Janet Yellen, a former chair of the Federal Reserve, for speeches, according to her disclosures. Barclays is also named in a case where Bank of England deputy Hogg failed to declare her brother's Barclays role. A Treasury Committee report called that a very serious breach, and she resigned on 14 March 2017.
n:Attorney-General of Ghana: The Attorney-General of Ghana is an agency based in Accra. In February 2020 it charged Duffuor, a former finance minister and former governor of the Bank of Ghana, and seven others with 68 counts over the collapse of uniBank. Duffuor was charged with dishonestly receiving 663.28 million Ghana cedi and money laundering. Asiama, a former second deputy governor of the Bank of Ghana, was accused of using his position to approve the transfer of a 300 million cedi unsecured credit facility from distressed uniBank to Universal Merchant Bank. These are charges and accusations, and no outcome is given.
n:Kwabena Duffuor: Kwabena Duffuor is a person based in Accra, Ghana, and a former finance minister and former governor of the Bank of Ghana. In February 2020 Ghana's Attorney-General charged him and seven others with 68 counts over the collapse of uniBank. He was charged with dishonestly receiving 663.28 million Ghana cedi and money laundering. Former second deputy governor Asiama was accused of using his position to approve the transfer of a 300 million cedi unsecured credit facility from distressed uniBank to Universal Merchant Bank. The charges are unproven, and no outcome is given.
n:uniBank: uniBank is a bank based in Accra, Ghana. It is named in a documented case involving the Bank of Ghana, the country's central bank. In February 2020 Ghana's Attorney-General charged former finance minister and former Bank of Ghana governor Duffuor and seven others with 68 counts over uniBank's collapse. Former second deputy governor Asiama was accused of using his position to approve the transfer of a 300 million Ghana cedi unsecured credit facility from distressed uniBank to Universal Merchant Bank. The charges are unproven, and no outcome is given.
n:Universal Merchant Bank: Universal Merchant Bank is a bank based in Accra, Ghana. It is tied to the Bank of Ghana, the country's central bank, through a case over the collapse of uniBank. In February 2020 Ghana's Attorney-General charged former governor Duffuor and seven others with 68 counts. Former second deputy governor Asiama was accused of using his position to approve the transfer of a 300 million Ghana cedi unsecured credit facility from distressed uniBank to Universal Merchant Bank. The accusation is unproven, and no outcome is given.
n:Government of Ghana: The Government of Ghana is based in Accra and is tied to the Bank of Ghana, the country's central bank, in two ways. In a February 2023 statement the Bank of Ghana said its claims on government at December 2022 included a 37.9 billion Ghana cedi overdraft to cover auction shortfalls and pay maturing bonds, 7.2 billion cedi of treasury bonds bought from banks and 8.9 billion cedi of on-lent IMF funds. The government, the Bank of Ghana and the IMF had earlier adopted zero deficit financing. Separately, the Daily Graphic reported the government was pushing for second deputy governor Johnson Asiama to leave. His counsel alleged that some officials told him they wanted him to step aside. Asiama said he had not resigned. The article gives no official reason and no final outcome.
n:CRIEF (Guinea): CRIEF is a court based in Conakry, Guinea. On 23 June 2026 its appeals chamber convicted Bah, a former governor of the Central Bank of the Republic of Guinea, in his absence of embezzlement of public funds and related offences. It sentenced him to five years, ordered repayment of 10.5 million dollars taken from the central bank's coffers without trace, set a fine of 5 billion Guinean francs, and ordered confiscation of assets. His defence said the funds were released on instruction of the highest state authorities for an international humanitarian organisation.
n:Novartis: Novartis is a company based in Basel, Switzerland. It is tied to the Bank of Greece, Greece's central bank, through bribery allegations against its governor Stournaras. They were that he accepted bribes from Novartis while finance minister, and the allegations concerned 2001 onward, before his central bank post. On 29 August 2019 Greek prosecutors dropped those charges, along with charges against six other former senior officials.
n:Greek prosecutors: Greek prosecutors are an agency based in Athens, Greece. They brought charges that Stournaras, now governor of the Bank of Greece, the country's central bank, accepted bribes from Novartis while finance minister. The allegations concerned 2001 onward and predated his central bank post. On 29 August 2019 the prosecutors dropped those charges, along with charges against six other former senior officials.
n:Honduran prosecutors: Honduran prosecutors are an agency based in Tegucigalpa, Honduras. On 3 June 2026 they charged 11 current and former employees of the Banco Central de Honduras, the country's central bank, two of them serving managers, with 100 counts of negligent embezzlement. The charges concern a scheme that allegedly removed public funds from the central bank over several years. The employees were arrested after the court admitted the case. The charges are unproven, and no outcome is given.
n:Zagreb prosecution: The Zagreb prosecution is an agency based in Zagreb, Croatia. In January 2022, after media reports, it and the market regulator HANFA opened probes into whether senior officials of the Croatian National Bank traded securities of supervised commercial banks using insider information. The central bank, the HNB, said its executives sold bank shares before the ban took effect and that bond trading was not prohibited. The probes are unproven allegations, and no outcome is given.
n:HANFA: HANFA is the market regulator, an agency based in Zagreb, Croatia. In January 2022, after media reports, it and the Zagreb prosecution opened probes into whether senior officials of the Croatian National Bank traded securities of supervised commercial banks using insider information. The central bank, the HNB, said its executives sold bank shares before the ban took effect and that bond trading was not prohibited. The probes are unproven allegations, and no outcome is given.
n:Constitutional Court of Hungary: The Constitutional Court of Hungary is a court based in Budapest. The Magyar Nemzeti Bank (MNB) is Hungary's central bank. It set up the Pallas Athéné foundations in 2014 and endowed them with a little over 267 billion forints. On 31 March 2016 the court ruled that the foundations were managing public funds subject to scrutiny. In June 2016 the Public Procurement Board then found that public procurement law applied to the six foundations and fined each 200,000 forints. The fine was minor because they had requested the review.
n:Public Procurement Board (Hungary): The Public Procurement Board is an agency based in Budapest, Hungary. The Magyar Nemzeti Bank (MNB) is Hungary's central bank. It set up the Pallas Athéné foundations in 2014 and endowed them with a little over 267 billion forints. After the Constitutional Court ruled on 31 March 2016 that the foundations were managing public funds subject to scrutiny, the Board found in June 2016 that public procurement law applied to the six foundations. It fined each 200,000 forints, a minor fine because they had requested the review.
n:Pallas Athéné foundations: The Pallas Athéné foundations are six foundations in Budapest, Hungary, set up in 2014 as part of the Magyar Nemzeti Bank, Hungary's central bank, which endowed them with a little over 267 billion forints. On 31 March 2016 the Constitutional Court ruled they were managing public funds subject to scrutiny. In June 2016 the Public Procurement Board found that public procurement law applied to them and fined each 200,000 forints, a minor fine because they had requested the review. In March 2025 the State Audit Office published a 373-page report on the foundations. It found mismanagement of public funds, lack of oversight and losses of hundreds of billions of forints, and filed a criminal complaint over multiple suspected offences. The report focused on the Pallas Athéné Domus Meriti Foundation and its asset manager Optima. No outcome of the complaint is given.
n:State Audit Office of Hungary: The State Audit Office of Hungary is an agency based in Budapest. In March 2025 it published a 373-page report on the foundations controlled by the Magyar Nemzeti Bank, Hungary's central bank. It found mismanagement of public funds, lack of oversight and losses of hundreds of billions of forints. It filed a criminal complaint over multiple suspected offences. The report focused on the Pallas Athéné Domus Meriti Foundation and its asset manager Optima. The offences are suspected and unproven, and no outcome is given.
n:Optima: Optima is a company based in Budapest, Hungary. It is the asset manager of the Pallas Athéné Domus Meriti Foundation, one of the foundations controlled by the Magyar Nemzeti Bank, Hungary's central bank. In March 2025 the State Audit Office published a 373-page report on the foundations. It found mismanagement of public funds, lack of oversight and losses of hundreds of billions of forints, and filed a criminal complaint over multiple suspected offences. Optima is named in that case. The offences are suspected and unproven, and no outcome is given.
n:Ádám Matolcsy: Ádám Matolcsy is a person; the map marks Hungary as a whole. He is named in a documented case involving the Magyar Nemzeti Bank, Hungary's central bank. In March 2025 the State Audit Office published a 373-page report on the bank's controlled foundations. It found mismanagement of public funds, lack of oversight and losses of hundreds of billions of forints, and filed a criminal complaint over multiple suspected offences. The report focused on the Pallas Athéné Domus Meriti Foundation and its asset manager Optima. Being named in the case is not an accusation against him, and no outcome is given.
n:Central Chief Prosecution Office of In: This is a Hungarian state investigation agency based in Budapest. It is tied to Magyar Nemzeti Bank, Hungary's central bank. On 21 October 2026, according to his lawyer, the bank's former governor Matolcsy was detained and taken to this office on suspicion of economic fraud causing significant financial damage and use of a forged private document. A lawyer and a businessman, among others, were also detained. These are suspicions only and nothing is proven.
n:Supreme Court of Victoria: This is a court in Melbourne, Australia, tied to four central banks: Bank Indonesia, Bank Negara Malaysia, Nepal Rastra Bank and the State Bank of Vietnam. In October 2011 Securency and Note Printing Australia (NPA), subsidiaries of the Reserve Bank of Australia, pleaded guilty there to conspiring to provide benefits to foreign public officials to win banknote business with the note-issuing authorities of these countries. The periods were 1999 to 2001 for Indonesia, 2001 to 2003 for Malaysia, 2000 to 2002 for Nepal (NPA only) and 2001 to 2004 for Vietnam (Securency only). The officials are not named.
n:Corruption Court (Jakarta): This is the anti-corruption court in Jakarta, Indonesia, tied to Bank Indonesia, the country's central bank. In October 2008 it sentenced former governor Burhanuddin Abdullah to five years for approving the use of 100 billion rupiah of bank funds in 2003 to pay legal fees for officials in a graft case and to bribe legislators over an amendment to the bank's law. The Jakarta High Court raised this to five and a half years in February 2009. In July 2014 it sentenced Budi Mulya to 10 years and a 500 million rupiah fine for corruption in a 2008 loan to Bank Century.
n:Jakarta High Court: This is an appeals court in Jakarta, Indonesia, tied to Bank Indonesia, the country's central bank. In October 2008 the Corruption Court sentenced former governor Burhanuddin Abdullah to five years for approving the use of 100 billion rupiah of bank funds in 2003 to pay legal fees for officials in a graft case and to bribe legislators over an amendment to the bank's law. In February 2009 the Jakarta High Court raised the sentence to five and a half years.
n:Corruption Eradication Commission (KPK: The KPK is Indonesia's anti-corruption agency, based in Jakarta, and is tied to Bank Indonesia, the central bank. In November 2008 it arrested four former deputy governors of the bank, including Aulia Pohan, after former governor Burhanuddin Abdullah was sentenced to five years that October. In August 2025 it named two members of parliament's House as suspects in the alleged misuse of corporate social responsibility (CSR) funds from Bank Indonesia and the Financial Services Authority. These are allegations and nothing is proven.
n:Indonesian legislators: This is the group of Indonesian lawmakers, in Jakarta, tied to Bank Indonesia, the central bank. In October 2008 the Corruption Court sentenced former governor Burhanuddin Abdullah to five years, raised to five and a half by the Jakarta High Court in February 2009. He was sentenced for approving the use of 100 billion rupiah of bank funds in 2003 to pay legal fees for officials in a graft case and to bribe legislators over an amendment to the bank's law. In November 2008 the anti-corruption commission arrested four former deputy governors.
n:Bank Century: Bank Century is a bank in Jakarta, Indonesia, tied to Bank Indonesia, the central bank. In 2008 Bank Indonesia granted it a short-term loan facility of 689.39 billion rupiah and declared it a failed bank with systemic impact. In July 2014 the anti-corruption court sentenced Bank Indonesia's Budi Mulya to 10 years and a 500 million rupiah fine for corruption over that loan. The court put state losses at 8.5 trillion rupiah, including a 6.7 trillion rupiah bailout.
n:Robert Tantular: Robert Tantular was the owner of Bank Century in Indonesia. Bank Indonesia, the country's central bank, granted Bank Century a loan facility of 689.39 billion rupiah in 2008. In July 2014 the anti-corruption court sentenced Budi Mulya of the central bank to 10 years and a 500 million rupiah fine for corruption over that loan. The court found Mulya received a loan of 1 billion rupiah from Tantular.
n:Bank Indonesia employees' foundation: This is a foundation for the employees of Bank Indonesia, the central bank of Indonesia, based in Jakarta. It appears in a corruption case from 2008, when the bank gave a 689.39 billion rupiah loan facility to Bank Century and declared it a failed bank. In July 2014 the anti-corruption court sentenced Budi Mulya to 10 years and a 500 million rupiah fine. The court found he acted partly to save 83 billion rupiah deposited by the foundation.
n:Heri Gunawan: Heri Gunawan is linked to Bank Indonesia, the central bank of Indonesia, through a case in Jakarta. In August 2025 the Corruption Eradication Commission (KPK) named two members of parliament's House as suspects in the alleged misuse of corporate social responsibility (CSR) funds from Bank Indonesia and the Financial Services Authority. The funds were channelled after closed-door budget discussions in 2020 to 2022 by the commission that approves the bank's budget. These are allegations and nothing is proven.
n:Satori: Satori is linked to Bank Indonesia, the central bank of Indonesia, through a case in Jakarta. In August 2025 the Corruption Eradication Commission (KPK) named two members of parliament's House as suspects in the alleged misuse of corporate social responsibility (CSR) funds from Bank Indonesia and the Financial Services Authority. The funds were channelled after closed-door budget discussions in 2020 to 2022 by the commission that approves the bank's budget. These are allegations and nothing is proven.
n:House of Representatives Commission XI: This is a committee of Indonesia's House of Representatives, in Jakarta, that approves the budget of Bank Indonesia, the central bank. In August 2025 the anti-corruption commission (KPK) named two House members as suspects in the alleged misuse of corporate social responsibility (CSR) funds from Bank Indonesia and the Financial Services Authority. The funds were channelled after closed-door budget discussions in 2020 to 2022 by this commission. These are allegations and nothing is proven.
n:Financial Services Authority (OJK): The Financial Services Authority (OJK) is an Indonesian agency in Jakarta tied to Bank Indonesia, the central bank. In August 2025 the anti-corruption commission (KPK) named two House members as suspects in the alleged misuse of corporate social responsibility (CSR) funds from Bank Indonesia and the OJK. The funds were channelled after closed-door budget discussions in 2020 to 2022 by the House commission that approves the central bank's budget. These are allegations and nothing is proven.
n:Central Bureau of Investigation (India: This is India's federal investigation agency, based in New Delhi, tied to the Reserve Bank of India, the central bank. In December 2016, while the country was withdrawing 500 and 1,000 rupee notes (demonetisation), it arrested RBI official K. Michael in Bangalore. He is accused of converting 15 million rupees (about 222,000 dollars) of withdrawn notes into 100 rupee notes without legal documentation, working with a state bank employee. This is an allegation and no outcome is reported.
n:Salar Aghakhani: Salar Aghakhani is a Tehran-based intermediary tied to the Central Bank of the Islamic Republic of Iran. In October 2021 a Tehran court sentenced him to 13 years over an illegal foreign-currency distribution scheme in 2017 and 2018. Former governor Seif got 10 years and former deputy Araghchi eight. According to Iran Times, the Supreme Court overturned the verdicts in 2023, citing insufficient evidence and authorisation by higher authorities. The judiciary dropped the prosecution of Seif and Araghchi in March 2025.
n:Tehran court: This is a court in Tehran, Iran, tied to the Central Bank of the Islamic Republic of Iran. In October 2021 it sentenced former governor Seif to 10 years for taking part in disrupting the financial system through illegal smuggling of foreign currency, former deputy Araghchi to eight years and intermediary Salar Aghakhani to 13 years, over a currency distribution scheme in 2017 and 2018. According to Iran Times, the Supreme Court overturned the verdicts in 2023, and the judiciary dropped the prosecution of Seif and Araghchi in March 2025.
n:Supreme Court of Iran: This is Iran's highest court, in Tehran, tied to the Central Bank of the Islamic Republic of Iran. In October 2021 a Tehran court sentenced former governor Seif to 10 years, former deputy Araghchi to eight and intermediary Salar Aghakhani to 13, over an illegal foreign-currency distribution scheme in 2017 and 2018. According to Iran Times, the Supreme Court overturned the verdicts in 2023, citing insufficient evidence and authorisation by higher authorities. The judiciary dropped the prosecution of Seif and Araghchi in March 2025.
n:Iranian judiciary: This is Iran's court system, based in Tehran, tied to the Central Bank of the Islamic Republic of Iran. In October 2021 a Tehran court sentenced former governor Seif to 10 years, former deputy Araghchi to eight and intermediary Salar Aghakhani to 13, over an illegal foreign-currency distribution scheme in 2017 and 2018. The judiciary said 10 people were identified in the scheme. The Supreme Court overturned the verdicts in 2023, according to Iran Times, and the judiciary dropped the prosecution of Seif and Araghchi in March 2025.
n:Cabinet of Iraq: This is the government cabinet of Iraq, in Baghdad, tied to the Central Bank of Iraq. In October 2012 it removed governor Sinan al-Shabibi after a parliamentary committee charged that bank officials were abusing the bank's dollar sales. A successor was named, and a committee member said arrest warrants had been issued for 30 people, including al-Shabibi and his deputy Mudher Saleh. The Supreme Judicial Council confirmed warrants without giving charges. His defence called the case politically motivated; a finance committee member also called it a political decision.
n:Council of Representatives of Iraq (co: This is a committee of Iraq's parliament, in Baghdad, tied to the Central Bank of Iraq. In 2012 it investigated the bank over possible manipulation of the dinar against the dollar and charged that bank officials were abusing the bank's dollar sales. In October 2012 the cabinet removed governor al-Shabibi, and the Supreme Judicial Council confirmed arrest warrants for him and other officials without giving the charges. His defence called the case politically motivated.
n:Supreme Judicial Council (Iraq): This is Iraq's top judicial body, in Baghdad, tied to the Central Bank of Iraq. In October 2012 the cabinet removed the bank's governor al-Shabibi after a parliamentary committee charged that bank officials were abusing the bank's dollar sales. The Supreme Judicial Council then confirmed arrest warrants for him and other officials without giving the charges. His defence called the case politically motivated.
n:Board of Supreme Audit (Iraq): This is Iraq's state audit agency, in Baghdad, tied to the Central Bank of Iraq. In 2012 it investigated the central bank's daily dollar auctions and found that most transactions were based on fraudulent paperwork. According to the US Special Inspector General for Iraq Reconstruction, its top auditor told US officials that up to 800 million dollars a week was leaving Iraq illegally.
n:Special Inspector General for Iraq Rec: This is a United States oversight agency for Iraq reconstruction, tied to the Central Bank of Iraq. It reported that in 2012 Iraq's Board of Supreme Audit investigated the central bank's daily dollar auctions and found most transactions were based on fraudulent paperwork. According to the agency, the top auditor told US officials that up to 800 million dollars a week was leaving Iraq illegally.
n:Special Investigation Commission (Icel: This is a commission set up by Iceland's parliament, based in Reykjavik, tied to the Central Bank of Iceland. In April 2010 it found that seven officials, including central bank head Oddsson and central bank officials Gudnason and Fridriksson, acted with gross negligence before the 2008 collapse of Iceland's three largest banks. It said they failed to act on information about the banks' condition.
n:Banca Popolare di Lodi: Banca Popolare di Lodi is a bank in Lodi, Italy, tied to the Bank of Italy, the country's central bank. In 2005 it attempted to take over another bank, Antonveneta. On 28 May 2011 a Milan court sentenced former Bank of Italy governor Fazio to four years in prison and a fine of 1.5 million euros for market rigging in that attempt. Prosecutors argued he repeatedly favoured Fiorani's bank over ABN Amro by speeding some authorisations and slowing others.
n:Gianpiero Fiorani: Gianpiero Fiorani is tied to the Bank of Italy, the country's central bank, through a case centred on Lodi. In the 2005 attempted takeover of Antonveneta by Banca Popolare di Lodi, prosecutors argued that former Bank of Italy governor Fazio favoured Fiorani's bank over ABN Amro by speeding some authorisations and slowing others. On 28 May 2011 a Milan court sentenced Fazio to four years in prison and a fine of 1.5 million euros for market rigging.
n:ABN Amro: ABN Amro is a bank based in Amsterdam, tied to two central banks. For the Bank of England it is a former employer: Lord Jitesh Gadhia, now a Non-Executive Director of the Bank of England's Court, came from investment banking at Blackstone, Barclays Capital, ABN AMRO and Baring Brothers. For the Bank of Italy, it appears in a 2011 case in which a Milan court sentenced former governor Fazio for market rigging. Prosecutors argued he favoured Banca Popolare di Lodi over ABN Amro in a 2005 takeover contest.
n:Antonveneta: Antonveneta is a bank in Padua, Italy, tied to the Bank of Italy, the country's central bank. It was the target of an attempted takeover by Banca Popolare di Lodi in 2005. On 28 May 2011 a Milan court sentenced former Bank of Italy governor Fazio to four years in prison and a fine of 1.5 million euros for market rigging in that attempt. Prosecutors argued he favoured Lodi's bank over ABN Amro.
n:Milan court: This is a court in Milan, Italy, tied to the Bank of Italy, the country's central bank. On 28 May 2011 it sentenced former governor Fazio to four years in prison and a fine of 1.5 million euros for market rigging in the 2005 attempted takeover of Antonveneta by Banca Popolare di Lodi. In October 2011 Fazio was sentenced to three and a half years at first instance over Unipol's attempted 2005 takeover of BNL. On 30 May 2012 the Milan Court of Appeal acquitted him and 12 other defendants of market rigging.
n:Unipol: Unipol is an insurance and finance company in Bologna, Italy, tied to the Bank of Italy, the country's central bank. It attempted to take over the bank BNL in 2005. In October 2011 former Bank of Italy governor Fazio was sentenced to three and a half years at first instance over that attempt. On 30 May 2012 the Milan Court of Appeal acquitted him and 12 other defendants of market rigging.
n:BNL: BNL is a bank in Rome, Italy, tied to the Bank of Italy, the country's central bank. Unipol attempted to take it over in 2005. In October 2011 former Bank of Italy governor Fazio was sentenced to three and a half years at first instance over that attempt. On 30 May 2012 the Milan Court of Appeal acquitted him and 12 other defendants of market rigging.
n:Milan Court of Appeal: This is an appeals court in Milan, Italy, tied to the Bank of Italy, the country's central bank. Former governor Fazio was sentenced in October 2011 to three and a half years at first instance over Unipol's attempted 2005 takeover of the bank BNL. On 30 May 2012 the Milan Court of Appeal acquitted him and 12 other defendants of market rigging.
n:Yoshiaki Murakami: Yoshiaki Murakami is linked to the Bank of Japan, the country's central bank, through a fund he ran. In June 2006 Bank of Japan chief Fukui apologised and took a 30 percent pay cut for six months after disclosing he had kept an investment of 10 million yen, made in 1999, in that fund. Murakami was arrested for insider trading, and the stake had grown to 22 million yen. The bank said Fukui broke no law or internal rule, and he did not resign.
n:Wilfred Koinange: Wilfred Koinange, based in Nairobi, is named in the Goldenberg case involving the Central Bank of Kenya. The government paid cash subsidies for fictitious gold and diamond exports by Goldenberg International under President Moi. A judicial inquiry reported in February 2006. In March 2006 prosecutors indicted five people, including former governor Kotut and former deputy governor Riungu. Earlier proceedings against Riungu had been halted.
n:Kamlesh Pattni: Kamlesh Pattni is named in the Goldenberg case involving the Central Bank of Kenya. In that scandal the government paid cash subsidies for fictitious gold and diamond exports by Goldenberg International under President Moi. A judicial inquiry reported in February 2006. In March 2006 Kenyan prosecutors indicted five people, including former governor Kotut and former deputy governor Riungu. Earlier proceedings against Riungu had been halted.
n:Goldenberg International: Goldenberg International is a company in Nairobi, Kenya, named in a case involving the Central Bank of Kenya. Under President Moi, the government paid cash subsidies for fictitious gold and diamond exports by the company, in what became known as the Goldenberg scandal. A judicial inquiry reported in February 2006. In March 2006 Kenyan prosecutors indicted five people, including former governor Kotut and former deputy governor Riungu. Earlier proceedings against Riungu had been halted.
n:Daniel arap Moi: Daniel arap Moi was president of Kenya when, in the Goldenberg scandal, the government paid cash subsidies for fictitious gold and diamond exports by Goldenberg International. He is named in the case, which involves the Central Bank of Kenya. A judicial inquiry reported in February 2006. In March 2006 Kenyan prosecutors indicted five people, including former governor Kotut and former deputy governor Riungu. Earlier proceedings against Riungu had been halted.
n:Kenyan prosecutors: These are the state prosecutors of Kenya, based in Nairobi, tied to the Central Bank of Kenya. In March 2006 they indicted five people, including former governor Kotut and former deputy governor Riungu, over the Goldenberg scandal. In it, the government paid cash subsidies for fictitious gold and diamond exports by Goldenberg International under President Moi. A judicial inquiry had reported in February 2006. Earlier proceedings against Riungu had been halted.
n:Kenyan judicial inquiry: This is a judicial inquiry in Kenya, in Nairobi, tied to the Central Bank of Kenya. It reported in February 2006 on the Goldenberg scandal, in which the government paid cash subsidies for fictitious gold and diamond exports by Goldenberg International under President Moi. In March 2006 prosecutors indicted five people, including former central bank governor Kotut and former deputy governor Riungu. Earlier proceedings against Riungu had been halted.
n:Silla Mullei: Silla Mullei was governor of the Central Bank of Kenya. On 23 March 2006 he was charged with four counts of abuse of office. They included appointing his son as a bank consultant without following procurement procedures, with the son paid 2,619,154.85 shillings in fees, and improperly appointing three other consultants. He denied awarding 9 million shillings in contracts irregularly and was freed on 5 million shillings bail. The charges are unproven.
n:Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission: This is Kenya's anti-corruption agency, in Nairobi, tied to the Central Bank of Kenya. It said it was investigating former and current central bank officials over their role in the accounting fraud that brought down Imperial Bank. In August 2018 Imperial Bank's directors told a parliamentary committee that central bank officers took part in the 34 billion shilling embezzlement by manipulating the bank's IT systems. These are allegations and nothing is proven.
n:Imperial Bank: Imperial Bank was a bank in Nairobi, Kenya, that collapsed after an accounting fraud, and it is tied to the Central Bank of Kenya. In August 2018 its directors told a parliamentary committee that central bank officers took part in the 34 billion shilling embezzlement by manipulating the bank's IT systems. Kenya's Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission said it was investigating former and current central bank officials over their role. These are allegations and nothing is proven.
n:Kenyan National Assembly committee: This is a committee of Kenya's National Assembly, in Nairobi, tied to the Central Bank of Kenya. In August 2018 the directors of Imperial Bank, which had collapsed after an accounting fraud, told it that central bank officers took part in the 34 billion shilling embezzlement by manipulating the bank's IT systems. Kenya's Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission said it was investigating former and current central bank officials. These are allegations and nothing is proven.
n:Askar Akayev: Askar Akayev is the deposed president of Kyrgyzstan. In September 2005 prosecutors placed the governor of the National Bank of the Kyrgyz Republic, Sarbanov, under house arrest, accusing him of abuse of power for handing out more than 400,000 dollars to Akayev in 1999. Sarbanov denied wrongdoing. No outcome is reported.
n:Kyrgyz prosecutors: These are the state prosecutors of Kyrgyzstan, based in Bishkek, tied to the National Bank of the Kyrgyz Republic, the central bank. In September 2005 they placed governor Sarbanov under house arrest. They accused him of abuse of power for handing out more than 400,000 dollars to deposed president Askar Akayev in 1999. Sarbanov denied wrongdoing, and the accusation is unproven.
n:Vientiane People's Court: This is a court in Vientiane, Laos, tied to the Bank of the Lao P.D.R., the country's central bank. On 8 September 2026 it sentenced two former directors general of the bank to life imprisonment. One, Aod, was sentenced in his absence because he died during the proceedings. They were convicted of abusing their positions to withdraw foreign currency from the bank's reserves and exchange unlimited amounts. In a related case nine bank employees were convicted of corruption and money laundering, including trading currency at special rates. Losses across the cases exceeded 2.29 trillion kip (102.6 million dollars).
n:French prosecutors: These are state prosecutors in Paris, tied to Banque du Liban, Lebanon's central bank. Its governor for three decades until 2023, Riad Salameh, was investigated over allegations that more than 300 million dollars was siphoned off between 2002 and 2015 through Forry Associates, a company controlled by his brother Raja. In May 2023 they issued an arrest warrant after he failed to appear for questioning in a joint French, German and Luxembourg probe into illicit enrichment and alleged laundering of 330 million dollars. Germany issued a second warrant the following week. Salameh was later arrested in Beirut on charges of embezzlement, money laundering and fraud. He and his brother deny wrongdoing, and the charges are unproven.
n:German authorities: These are German state authorities tied to Banque du Liban, Lebanon's central bank. They took part in a joint French, German and Luxembourg probe into illicit enrichment and alleged laundering of 330 million dollars involving former governor Riad Salameh. In May 2023, the week after France issued an arrest warrant, Germany issued a second one on charges including corruption, forgery, money laundering and embezzlement. Salameh called the French warrant a violation of the law. He was later arrested in Beirut and denies wrongdoing. The charges are unproven.
n:Luxembourg authorities: These are Luxembourg state authorities tied to Banque du Liban, Lebanon's central bank. They took part in a joint French, German and Luxembourg judicial probe into illicit enrichment and alleged laundering of 330 million dollars involving former governor Riad Salameh. In May 2023 French prosecutors issued an arrest warrant for Salameh after he failed to appear for questioning, and Germany issued a second warrant the following week. Salameh called the French warrant a violation of the law.
n:Raja Salameh: Raja Salameh is the brother of Riad Salameh, who was governor of Banque du Liban, Lebanon's central bank, for three decades until 2023. Investigators allege that more than 300 million dollars was siphoned off between 2002 and 2015 through Forry Associates, a company Raja controlled, which is suspected of receiving commissions from commercial banks and transferring them abroad. Investigations are open in France, Germany, Switzerland and other countries. Both brothers deny wrongdoing, and nothing is proven.
n:Forry Associates: Forry Associates is a company based in Road Town, British Virgin Islands, controlled by Raja Salameh, brother of Riad Salameh, who was governor of Banque du Liban, Lebanon's central bank. Investigators allege that more than 300 million dollars was siphoned off between 2002 and 2015 through it. The company is suspected of receiving commissions from commercial banks and transferring them abroad. Investigations are open in France, Germany, Switzerland and other countries. Both brothers deny wrongdoing, and nothing is proven.
n:Lebanese state investigation: This is the Lebanese state investigation, in Beirut, into former Banque du Liban governor Riad Salameh. n:Alvarez & Marsal: Alvarez & Marsal is a consulting firm based in New York, United States. n:Shulman Rogers: Shulman Rogers is a law firm based in Potomac, United States. It is named in a case involving the Central Bank of Somalia. Governor Abrar resigned after seven weeks and wrote to the president that since her appointment she had 'continuously been asked to sanction deals and violate my fiduciary responsibility'. She said she had refused to sanction a contract over frozen government assets with Shulman Rogers. The firm denied wrongdoing.
n:Serbian police: Serbian police are the national police, based in Belgrade. In January 2006 they arrested Dejan Simić, vice-governor of the National Bank of Serbia, on suspicion of taking bribes, according to the news agency Mina. No outcome is given, so the suspicion is unproven.
n:De La Rue: De La Rue is a banknote printer based in Basingstoke, United Kingdom, tied to eight central banks. It prints notes for the Bank of England (a 500 million pound contract decided 29 September 2014, extended to 2028), Kenya, Sweden, Libya, South Sudan, Tanzania and, per a trial witness, historically for Nigeria. In South Sudan, a UN report said it sent about 1.4 million dollars between 2016 and September 2017 to a Nairobi account held by a Bank of South Sudan consultant, against a contract worth about 144 million dollars, and noted 'suspected corruption'. The UK Serious Fraud Office opened an investigation in July 2019 and closed it in June 2020 without charges. In September 2010 De La Rue said some employees had falsified banknote paper test certificates, followed by a supply suspension to the Reserve Bank of India.
n:Equity Bank: Equity Bank is a bank based in Nairobi, Kenya. It is named in a case involving the Bank of South Sudan. A UN Human Rights Council commission report said the banknote printer De La Rue transferred about 1.4 million dollars to an Equity Bank account in Nairobi held by a Bank of South Sudan consultant between 2016 and September 2017. The transfers were set against a banknote contract worth about 144 million dollars, and the report noted 'suspected corruption'. The UK Serious Fraud Office closed its own investigation into De La Rue in June 2020 without charges.
n:UN Commission on Human Rights in South: The UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan is a United Nations body based in Geneva, Switzerland. Its report to the UN Human Rights Council said the banknote printer De La Rue transferred about 1.4 million dollars to an Equity Bank account in Nairobi held by a Bank of South Sudan consultant between 2016 and September 2017. The transfers were set against a banknote contract worth about 144 million dollars, and the report noted 'suspected corruption'. The UK Serious Fraud Office closed its own investigation into De La Rue in June 2020 without charges.
n:South Sudan security forces: South Sudan's security forces are based in Juba. In February and March 2026 they detained former Bank of South Sudan governor Manguak, placing him under house arrest, along with former finance ministers and other officials. The information minister said a committee was investigating 'financial malpractices'. No charges had been publicly announced as of March 2026, and Manguak denies the allegations.

n:Surinamese court: The Surinamese court is a criminal court in Paramaribo, Suriname, that heard two cases tied to the Central Bank of Suriname. On 17 December 2021 it sentenced Hoefdraad, a former finance minister, in his absence to 12 years and a fine of 500,000 Surinamese dollars for a conspiracy to defraud the central bank. On 31 January 2022 it convicted former governor van Trikt of corruption, forgery, embezzlement, money laundering and taking part in a criminal enterprise, in a case involving over 800,000 dollars. It gave him eight years and the same fine, and the bank's legal director and others were also convicted. On appeal in January 2026 Hoefdraad's term became 10 years and van Trikt's became six. Hoefdraad, who left Suriname in 2020, calls his case a political show trial.
n:Surinamese Court of Appeal: The Surinamese Court of Appeal is based in Paramaribo, Suriname. On 19 January 2026 it ruled on Hoefdraad, a former finance minister sentenced in his absence in December 2021 to 12 years for a conspiracy to defraud the Central Bank of Suriname. It set 10 years for violating the anti-corruption law and embezzlement and dropped the criminal-organisation count. Hoefdraad, who left Suriname in 2020, called the case a political show trial. In January 2026 van Trikt's sentence, originally eight years, was also reduced to six years on appeal.

n:Specialised Criminal Court (Slovakia): The Specialised Criminal Court is a Slovak court based in Pezinok. It fined him 200,000 euros. The offence predates his central bank post. He denied wrongdoing and said he would appeal.
n:Turkmenistan prosecutor's office: The Turkmenistan prosecutor's office is a state prosecution agency based in Ashgabat. No outcome is given, so the accusation is unproven.
n:Tunisian prosecutors: Tunisian prosecutors are based in Tunis. In February 2018 they said five agents of the Banque Centrale de Tunisie had been arrested, two of them jailed, in a currency-trafficking investigation. The agents were accused of money laundering, corruption and abuse of power for exchanging small euro notes for 200 and 500 euro notes without recording the operations. The central bank said it had itself referred the illegal operations to the courts. No outcome is given, so the accusations are unproven.
n:Istanbul prosecutors: Istanbul prosecutors are based in Istanbul, Türkiye. In October 2025 they took Şener, a former deputy governor of the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye, and six others into custody, and he was arrested. The case is a corruption and tender-rigging investigation into two 2023 tenders at the Interbank Card Center (BKM), the national payment network in which the central bank holds a majority stake. No outcome is given, so the allegations are unproven.

n:Jakaya Kikwete: Jakaya Kikwete was president of Tanzania. An Ernst & Young audit of the Bank of Tanzania's External Payment Arrears account found about 133 billion Tanzanian shillings paid wrongly in 2005/06 to 22 local companies, many of them phoney or using fake documents. In January 2008 Kikwete dismissed the bank's governor, Ballali. The companies were ordered to refund the money, and some lower-level defendants were jailed.

n:National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukr: The National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine is the country's main anti-graft agency, based in Kyiv. On 11 November 2019 it detained seven people, including Pysaruk, a former first deputy governor of the National Bank of Ukraine, and current and former bank officials. The suspicion is that they embezzled 1.2 billion hryvnia (about 49 million dollars) of a 2014 stabilisation loan from the bank to VAB Bank, which was declared insolvent in November 2014. No outcome is given, so the suspicion is unproven.
n:VAB Bank: VAB Bank is a bank based in Kyiv, Ukraine. In 2014 it received a stabilisation loan from the National Bank of Ukraine, and it was declared insolvent in November 2014. On 11 November 2019 Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau detained seven people, including former first deputy governor Pysaruk and current and former central bank officials, on suspicion of embezzling 1.2 billion hryvnia (about 49 million dollars) of that loan. n:Medley Global Advisors: Medley Global Advisors is a company based in New York, United States. In April 2017 Lacker resigned with immediate effect as head of the Richmond Federal Reserve Bank. He said that in October 2012 he spoke with a Medley analyst who held confidential information on options discussed at the September 2012 meeting of the Fed's policy committee, and that he may have confirmed it. He said he had not disclosed this in a 2012 internal inquiry. His lawyer said the investigation was complete and no charges would be brought.
n:Federal Reserve Office of Inspector Ge: The Federal Reserve Office of Inspector General is the Fed's internal watchdog, based in Washington. A report issued on 11 September 2024 found that trades made on Bostic's behalf from 2017 for about five years, including several during blackout periods before policy meetings, violated Fed ethics policies and created the appearance of acting on confidential information. It found no violation of insider trading or conflict of interest laws. It found no evidence that Powell's December 2019 trades or Clarida's 2020 trades broke laws, rules or policies then in effect, and made no law enforcement referral. Its January 2024 report said Kaplan's 2020 trading gave an appearance of acting on confidential information, and that Rosengren failed to report multiple trades. A 15 November 2025 ethics office report on Kugler's 2024 stock trades followed a Fed referral to it.
n:US Office of Government Ethics: The US Office of Government Ethics is a federal agency based in Washington. After a Federal Reserve referral to its inspector general, it released a report on 15 November 2025 on Kugler, a former Fed governor. Kugler's 2024 financial disclosure listed more than a dozen individual stock trades, several during blackout periods before policy meetings. The report said these violated Fed rules barring officials from holding individual stocks. The largest was an April 2024 Apple purchase of 100,000 to 250,000 dollars.
n:Apple: Apple is a technology company based in Cupertino, United States. It is tied to the Federal Reserve through stock held by an official. A report released on 15 November 2025 by the US Office of Government Ethics, after a Fed referral to its inspector general, covered former Fed governor Kugler's 2024 financial disclosure. It listed more than a dozen individual stock trades, several during blackout periods before policy meetings, which violated Fed rules barring officials from holding individual stocks. The largest was an April 2024 purchase of Apple stock worth 100,000 to 250,000 dollars. The tie is the stock, not wrongdoing by Apple.
n:Truong My Lan: Truong My Lan is the chair of the company Van Thinh Phat, based in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. In April 2024 Ho Chi Minh City People's Court sentenced her to death for fraud at Saigon Commercial Bank. The court found she ordered subordinates to bribe State Bank of Vietnam inspectors. State media said head banking inspector Do Thi Nhan received 5.2 million dollars in bribes and deputy chief inspector Nguyen Van Hung received 300,000 dollars.

n:UN Panel of Experts on Yemen: The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen is a United Nations expert body based in New York, United States. Its January 2021 report said the Aden-based Central Bank of Yemen broke its foreign-exchange rules and laundered a substantial part of a 2 billion dollar Saudi deposit, giving traders a 423 million dollar windfall. The bank rejected the claims. On 25 March 2021, after an internal review, the panel told the government it had withdrawn the money-laundering and corruption accusations, according to a Yemeni official quoted by Arab News.
n:Saudi Arabia: Saudi Arabia is a country whose government is based in Riyadh. It is tied to the Central Bank of Yemen through a 2 billion dollar Saudi deposit. In January 2021 a United Nations Panel of Experts report said the Aden-based central bank broke its foreign-exchange rules and laundered a substantial part of that deposit, giving traders a 423 million dollar windfall. The bank rejected the claims. On 25 March 2021, after an internal review, the panel told the government it withdrew the money-laundering and corruption accusations, according to a Yemeni official quoted by Arab News.
n:Absa: Absa is a bank based in Johannesburg, South Africa. It is tied to the South African Reserve Bank, the country's central bank, through an apartheid-era rescue loan the Reserve Bank gave to another bank, Bankorp. In June 2017 the Public Protector, a South African state watchdog, ordered Absa to repay 1.125 billion rand for that rescue. On 16 February 2018 the Pretoria High Court set aside the Public Protector's report and its orders, after the Reserve Bank and Absa asked for a review. The court also ordered the Public Protector to pay part of the Reserve Bank's costs personally.
n:Bankorp: Bankorp is a bank in South Africa. It is tied to the South African Reserve Bank, the country's central bank, through an apartheid-era rescue loan the Reserve Bank gave it. n:Robert Mugabe: Robert Mugabe, based in Harare, was president of Zimbabwe. He is named in a case involving the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe, the country's central bank. Under its governor Gono, the bank ran what are called quasi-fiscal activities, meaning spending that normally belongs to the government. These included cash for state enterprises and farm equipment handed out at events presided over by Mugabe. The bank also raided private foreign-currency accounts to fund state operations, leaving debts of close to 1.3 billion dollars. In 2014 the government tabled a bill to move that debt to taxpayers.
n:Government of Zimbabwe: The Government of Zimbabwe sits in Harare. It is tied to the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe, the country's central bank, as a recipient of its money. Under governor Gono the bank ran what are called quasi-fiscal activities, meaning spending that normally belongs to the government. These included cash for state enterprises and farm equipment handed out at events presided over by President Mugabe. The bank also raided private foreign-currency accounts to fund state operations, leaving debts of close to 1.3 billion dollars. In 2014 the government tabled the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe (Debt Assumption) Bill to move the debt to taxpayers.
n:Sakunda Holdings: Sakunda Holdings is a company in Harare, Zimbabwe, owned by Kudakwashe Tagwirei, who is described as an ally of the president. It received money from the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe, the country's central bank. At a September 2019 parliamentary Public Accounts Committee hearing, deputy governor Mlambo confirmed the bank issued 663.8 million dollars in Treasury Bills to Sakunda in 2017 and 2018 for the Command Agriculture programme, on instruction from the Finance Ministry. The committee also cited a 1.37 billion dollar overdraft issued by December 2017 without parliamentary approval. It could not get an explanation for 2.9 billion dollars paid from unallocated reserves in 2017.

n:BlackRock: BlackRock is an asset manager based in New York, meaning a firm that invests money for clients. Philipp Hildebrand moved from chairman of the Swiss National Bank's governing board, a post he held until January 2012, to vice chairman of BlackRock, and he represents it in the Group of Thirty, a forum where central bankers also sit. Stanley Fischer moved from Federal Reserve vice chair to senior adviser at BlackRock. BlackRock also managed money for the Federal Reserve: it was manager of the Primary and Secondary Market Corporate Credit Facilities, with agreements dated 29 June 2020, and of agency commercial mortgage-backed securities purchases under an agreement dated 25 March 2020. The European Central Bank selected it as a consultant to design its asset-backed securities purchase programme.
n:UBS: A bank based in Zurich, Switzerland, tied to two central banks. Axel Weber, Bundesbank president until April 2011, became chairman of UBS. The source also lists UBS as paying a former Federal Reserve official, Janet Yellen (Fed chair until early 2018), for speeches or advice, as shown in her disclosed speaking income reported in January 2021.
n:Commerzbank: A bank based in Frankfurt, Germany, tied to the Deutsche Bundesbank. Jens Weidmann, a former Bundesbank president, became chairman of Commerzbank's supervisory board.
n:Goldman Sachs: Goldman Sachs is a bank based in New York. Many people have moved between it and central banks. Mario Draghi was vice chairman and managing director of Goldman Sachs International from 2002 to 2005, then became governor of Banca d'Italia and later European Central Bank president. Otmar Issing went from European Central Bank chief economist to Goldman adviser. Hafize Gaye Erkan became governor of Türkiye's central bank from June 2023. Federal Reserve officials who came from Goldman include William Dudley, Neel Kashkari, Beth Hammack and Robert Kaplan. Bank of England officials Huw Pill and Ben Broadbent also worked there. Janet Yellen, a former Fed chair, was paid for speeches by Goldman, according to her disclosures. These are career moves, not accusations.
n:Brookfield Asset Management: Brookfield Asset Management is an investment company based in Toronto, Canada. It is tied to the Bank of England through shared people. Mark Carney, a former governor of the Bank of England and the Bank of Canada, became vice chair of Brookfield after leaving the Bank of England. Diana Noble sits on the Bank of England's Court, its board of directors, as a non-executive director and deputy chair, and also holds a board seat at Brookfield. These are career moves and board roles, not accusations.
n:First Republic Bank: A bank based in San Francisco, United States, tied to the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye. Hafize Gaye Erkan, governor from June 2023, came from Goldman Sachs, where she was a managing director, and First Republic Bank, where she was co-CEO.
n:Carlyle Group: A firm based in Washington, United States, tied to the Federal Reserve through two people. Jerome Powell was a partner at The Carlyle Group (1997-2005) before becoming a Fed governor; he was chair from February 2018 to May 2026 per the Fed biography. Randal Quarles moved from roles at The Carlyle Group to Fed vice chair for supervision (2017-2021).
n:Morgan Stanley: A bank based in New York, tied to the Federal Reserve and the Bank of England through three people. Kevin Warsh went from Morgan Stanley mergers and acquisitions (vice president and executive director) via the White House to Fed governor. David Miles, Chief UK Economist at Morgan Stanley, became a Bank of England Monetary Policy Committee member, as did Kristin Forbes, who was at Morgan Stanley before an academic post at MIT.
n:White House National Economic Council: A US government body in Washington tied to the Federal Reserve through one person: Kevin Warsh, a former Fed governor, who went from Morgan Stanley mergers and acquisitions (vice president and executive director) via the White House to the Fed board.
n:Warburg Pincus: A private equity firm based in New York, tied to the Federal Reserve through one person: Timothy Geithner, former New York Fed president and Treasury Secretary, who became president of Warburg Pincus.
n:US Treasury: The US Treasury, in Washington, tied to the Federal Reserve through one person: Timothy Geithner, who was New York Fed president, then Treasury Secretary, and then became president of the private equity firm Warburg Pincus.
n:Citadel: A hedge fund based in Miami, United States, tied to the Federal Reserve through two former officials. Ben Bernanke, former Fed chair, joined it as senior adviser. The source also lists Citadel as paying Janet Yellen (Fed chair until early 2018) for speeches or advice, as shown in her disclosed speaking income reported in January 2021.
n:Millennium Management: Millennium Management is an investment firm based in New York. It is tied to the Federal Reserve, the United States central bank, through one person. Randal Quarles, who was Fed vice chair for supervision from 2017 to 2021, moved from roles at The Carlyle Group to that Fed post, and Millennium Management employed him before or after his time at the Fed. This is a career move, not an accusation.
n:Donald Trump: Donald Trump is the president of the United States, based in Washington. He is tied to the Federal Reserve, the country's central bank, through pressure on its leaders. On 3 July 2025 he wrote on Truth Social that Fed Chair Jerome Powell should resign immediately. After reports that Trump was likely to fire Powell, he said it was highly unlikely unless Powell had to leave for fraud, referring to cost overruns in the 2.5 billion dollar renovation of Fed headquarters. Trump also announced he had fired Fed Governor Lisa Cook for cause over mortgage fraud allegations. Cook said no cause exists and sued on 28 August 2025. The D.C. Circuit on 15 September 2025 and the Supreme Court on 1 October 2025 refused emergency requests to remove her while the case continues. The Supreme Court later ruled 5-4 that she can stay on the Board while her challenge proceeds.
n:William Pulte: William Pulte is director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency and is based in Washington. He is tied to the Federal Reserve, the United States central bank, through pressure on its chair. President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social, in a post of 3 July 2025, that Fed Chair Jerome Powell should resign immediately, and shared an article about Pulte urging Congress to investigate Powell. No result of that call is recorded.
n:US Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circu: The US Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit is a federal court in Washington. It is named in a case involving the Federal Reserve, the United States central bank. President Trump announced he had fired Fed Governor Lisa Cook for cause over mortgage fraud allegations. Cook said no cause exists and sued on 28 August 2025. On 15 September 2025 the D.C. Circuit refused an emergency request to remove her while the litigation continues. The Supreme Court did the same on 1 October 2025.
n:Supreme Court of the United States: The Supreme Court of the United States is the country's highest court, in Washington. It is named in a case involving the Federal Reserve, the United States central bank. President Trump announced he had fired Fed Governor Lisa Cook for cause over mortgage fraud allegations, and Cook sued on 28 August 2025. On 1 October 2025 the Supreme Court refused an emergency request to remove her while the case continues. It later ruled 5-4 in Trump v. Cook that she can remain on the Fed Board while her challenge proceeds, holding that the law's for-cause protection entitles a governor to notice and a chance to respond.
n:White House Council of Economic Advise: The White House Council of Economic Advisers is a presidential advisory body in Washington. It is named in an event involving the Federal Reserve, the United States central bank. Stephen Miran, who chaired the Council, was sworn in as a Fed governor after a 48-47 Senate vote, filling the seat of Adriana Kugler. He was the first Fed member to serve at the same time in the executive branch since the 1930s. He resigned from the Council on 3 February 2026.
n:US Senate: The US Senate is the upper chamber of the United States Congress, in Washington. It is named in an event involving the Federal Reserve, the country's central bank. Stephen Miran, chair of the White House Council of Economic Advisers, was sworn in as a Fed governor after a 48-47 Senate vote, filling the seat of Adriana Kugler. He was the first Fed member to serve at the same time in the executive branch since the 1930s. He resigned from the Council on 3 February 2026.
n:US Department of Justice: The US Department of Justice is the federal law enforcement agency, based in Washington. It is tied to the Federal Reserve, the country's central bank, through a criminal inquiry. The Department served the Fed with grand jury subpoenas threatening a criminal indictment related to Chair Jerome Powell's June 2025 Senate testimony on the renovation of Fed buildings. In a statement on 11 January 2026, Powell said the action should be seen in the context of the administration's threats and pressure. No indictment is reported.
n:White House: The White House, in Washington, listed as having pressured or dismissed Federal Reserve officials. It notified Fed Governor Lisa Cook that President Trump was "considering" firing her and gave her three weeks to respond.
n:Recep Tayyip Erdoğan: Recep Tayyip Erdoğan is the president of Türkiye, based in Ankara. He dismissed three governors of the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye by decree. In July 2019 a decree replaced Murat Cetinkaya, whose term ran to 2020, with deputy Murat Uysal; Erdoğan said Cetinkaya had made decisions for which a high price was paid, after the bank held its rate at 24%. After the lira lost 30% of its value in 2020, he removed Uysal and appointed former finance minister Naci Agbal. On 20 March 2021 he removed Agbal after four months, following an interest rate rise, and appointed Sahap Kavcioglu, a banking professor who had argued for lower rates.
n:Presidency of Turkey: The Presidency of Turkey is the office of the president, in Ankara. It is tied to the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye through the replacement of a governor. Governor Sahap Kavcioglu, who had cut interest rates from 19% to 8.5%, was replaced by Hafize Gaye Erkan by presidential decree.
n:Presidential Council (Libya): The Presidential Council is a governing body based in Tripoli, Libya. It is tied to the Central Bank of Libya through the removal of its governor. In August 2024 it issued a decree replacing governor Sadiq al-Kabir, in post since October 2011, with former deputy governor Mohamed Abdul Salam al-Shukri. Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah's government then sent a delegation to take over the governor's office. Al-Kabir said he and other senior staff fled the country because of militia threats, and banking operations were suspended.
n:Government of National Unity (Libya): The Government of National Unity is the Tripoli-based government of Libya, led by Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah. It is tied to the Central Bank of Libya through a takeover of the governor's office. After the Presidential Council issued a decree in August 2024 replacing governor Sadiq al-Kabir, the government sent a delegation to take over his office. Al-Kabir said he and other senior staff fled the country because of militia threats, and banking operations were suspended.
n:UN Support Mission in Libya: The UN Support Mission in Libya is a United Nations mission based in Tripoli. It is named in an event involving the Central Bank of Libya. Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah's government sent a delegation to take over the governor's office. Governor Sadiq al-Kabir said he and other senior staff fled the country because of militia threats, and banking operations were suspended.
n:Volodymyr Zelensky: Volodymyr Zelensky is the president of Ukraine, based in Kyiv. He is named in an event involving the National Bank of Ukraine, the country's central bank. Its governor, Yakiv Smolii, submitted his resignation to Zelensky and stated that systematic political pressure had been exerted on the bank.
n:Abdel Fattah al-Sisi: Abdel Fattah al-Sisi is the president of Egypt, based in Cairo. He is named in an event involving the Central Bank of Egypt. Governor Tarek Amer, in office since 2015 with a term due to run to 2023, resigned in August 2022, with the Egyptian pound at 19.1 to the dollar. Al-Sisi accepted the resignation and named him a presidential adviser.
n:Government of Iran: The Government of Iran is based in Tehran. It replaced the governor of the Central Bank of the Islamic Republic of Iran twice. President Hassan Rouhani's cabinet dismissed Valiollah Seif, in post since August 2013, and replaced him with Abdolnasser Hemati; the source gives no stated reason, though Rouhani thanked Seif for his service and named tackling illegal credit institutions a priority. On 30 May 2021 the cabinet dismissed Hemmati because he was a candidate in the 18 June presidential election, and replaced him with deputy Akbar Komijani.
n:Edgar Lungu: Edgar Lungu was president of Zambia, based in Lusaka. He dismissed Denny Kalyalya, governor of the Bank of Zambia, the country's central bank, in August 2020. This came less than a week after Kalyalya warned of economic difficulties. Lungu appointed Christopher Mvunga from the finance ministry in his place.
n:Lazarus Chakwera: Lazarus Chakwera is the president of Malawi, based in Lilongwe. Soon after being elected, he dismissed Dalitso Kabambe, governor of the Reserve Bank of Malawi, the country's central bank. He appointed Wilson Banda in his place on 8 July 2020.
n:Peter Mutharika: Peter Mutharika is the president of Malawi, based in Lilongwe. He is named in an event involving the Reserve Bank of Malawi, the country's central bank. He appointed Henry Mathanga as deputy governor. Mathanga had been dismissed by the bank after a disciplinary inquiry and faces criminal charges, which are unproven. Critics say the appointment breaches Section 16(2) of the bank's act. Nyasa Times reported the outrage on 11 January 2026.
n:Abdel Fattah al-Burhan: Abdel Fattah al-Burhan heads Sudan's Sovereignty Council. He dismissed Burai Al-Siddiq Ali Ahmed, governor of the Central Bank of Sudan, after a dispute over gold purchase and export rules, and appointed Amna Mirghani Hassan El Toum. Deputy governor Mohamed Osman Ahmed Mohamed Khair was dismissed less than two weeks later. Dabanga reported this on 29 October 2025.
n:State Administration Council (Myanmar): The State Administration Council is the military body that governs Myanmar, based in Naypyidaw. It took control of the Central Bank of Myanmar's leadership after the coup of 1 February 2021. Three days after the coup it appointed Than Than Swe deputy governor; she later became governor, replacing Than Nyein. Radio Free Asia reported in August 2022 that the junta also replaced a vice chairman with Maj. Gen. Zaw Myint Naing, two months after appointing six lieutenant colonels as deputy directors.
n:United States: The United States government is based in Washington. It is tied to three central banks. After the Taliban takeover of Afghanistan, it froze nearly 9.5 billion dollars of Da Afghanistan Bank assets, much of it held at the New York Federal Reserve, and stopped cash shipments. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Western countries immobilised Russian central bank assets, estimated at around 300 billion euros worldwide. For Lebanon, former Banque du Liban governor Riad Salameh, governor for three decades until 2023, was arrested in Beirut on charges of embezzlement, money laundering and fraud linked to commissions from the bank's dealings with a brokerage firm. He denies wrongdoing, and the charges are unproven.
n:Taliban: The Taliban is the government of Afghanistan, based in Kabul. It is named in an event involving Da Afghanistan Bank, the country's central bank. After the Taliban took over, the United States froze nearly 9.5 billion dollars of the bank's assets, much of it held at the New York Federal Reserve, and stopped cash shipments.
n:Joe Biden: Joe Biden was president of the United States, based in Washington. He froze or seized reserves of Da Afghanistan Bank, Afghanistan's central bank. On 11 February 2022 he signed an executive order to split 7 billion dollars of frozen Afghan central bank assets. Half, 3.5 billion dollars, was for Afghan relief, and 3.5 billion dollars was kept in the United States for litigation by US victims of terrorism.
n:European Union: The European Union is a political and economic union of European countries, based in Brussels. It is tied to the Bank of Russia, Russia's central bank, by freezing its reserves. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Western countries immobilised Russian central bank assets, estimated at around 300 billion euros worldwide. On 13 December 2025 the EU agreed to freeze 210 billion euros of those assets held in Europe indefinitely, using Article 122 of the EU treaty. This replaced six-monthly renewals that Hungary or Slovakia could veto.
n:G7: The G7 is a group of major economies; no location is recorded for it. It is tied to the Bank of Russia, Russia's central bank, by freezing its reserves. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Western countries immobilised Russian central bank assets under their jurisdictions, estimated at around 300 billion euros worldwide, according to a European Parliament research service paper of 8 September 2025.
n:United Kingdom: The United Kingdom government is based in London. It froze Bank of Russia reserves: after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Western countries immobilised Russian central bank assets, estimated at around 300 billion euros worldwide. It is also named in a Venezuelan case. On 29 July 2022 London's High Court ruled that Venezuelan supreme court judgments backing the Maduro-appointed central bank board should be disregarded, which kept more than 1 billion dollars of Venezuelan gold at the Bank of England out of Maduro's control. For Lebanon, former Banque du Liban governor Riad Salameh was arrested in Beirut on charges of embezzlement, money laundering and fraud linked to bank commissions. He denies wrongdoing, and the charges are unproven.
